# dragoman 0.3.10 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/dragoman/0.3.10

# dragoman

A web server for scholarly metadata with full [DOI Resolution](https://www.doi.org/the-identifier/resources/factsheets/doi-resolution-documentation) and [DOI content negotiation](https://citation.doi.org/docs.html). Send a DOI as the URL path; receive a redirect to the landing page or metadata in any supported format depending on the `Accept` header.

## Installation

### Prerequisites

- Rust 1.75+ ([rustup.rs](https://rustup.rs))

### Install

```
```
This builds a release binary and installs it to `~/.cargo/bin/dragoman`. Make sure `~/.cargo/bin` is on your `PATH` (the Rust installer adds this automatically).

## Local SQLite database

dragoman can serve metadata directly from a local SQLite database in the [commonmeta](https://commonmeta.org) format, bypassing the live Crossref/DataCite APIs. This dramatically reduces latency and API load for high-traffic deployments.

### Database format

The database is a SQLite3 file with a single `works` table whose columns map one-to-one to the commonmeta v1.0 schema. The `id` column is the canonical DOI URL (e.g. `https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.1234`). Complex fields (contributors, references, …) are stored as JSON text.

You can build a database from any commonmeta-supported source using the [commonmeta](https://github.com/front-matter/commonmeta-rs) CLI.

## Running the server

### Start

```
# Default port 3456
# Custom port
# With a local database
# Write a PID file so the process can be stopped later
# All options together
```
Options can also be supplied as environment variables (flags take precedence):

```
PORT=8080 COMMONMETA_DB=/data/commonmeta-2026-06-15.sqlite3 RUST_LOG=dragoman=debug
```
During development you can use `cargo run` in place of the installed binary:

```
# Run from the project root — the sqlite3 file in the root is loaded by filename
# Or with a full path
```
### Error: port already in use

If the chosen port is already in use, the server logs an error and exits:

```
ERROR dragoman: failed to bind  port=3456  error=Address already in use (os error 48)
```
Choose a different port with `--port` or stop the process that holds the port.

### Database file not found

If the resolved database path does not exist, dragoman logs a warning and starts without a local database, falling back to the live API for all requests:

```
WARN dragoman: sqlite file not found, running without local database  path=…
```
To use a local database, place the SQLite file at the platform default path or set `COMMONMETA_DB` to its location.

### Stop

```
# Stop using the default PID file location (/tmp/dragoman.pid)
# Stop using a custom PID file
```
`dragoman stop` sends `SIGTERM` to the running process. The server handles the signal gracefully: it finishes in-flight requests and removes the PID file before exiting. Pressing `Ctrl-C` has the same effect.

## CLI reference

```
dragoman <COMMAND>
Commands:
  start  Start the server (runs in the foreground)
  stop   Stop a running server by sending SIGTERM to its PID file
  help   Print help
dragoman start [OPTIONS]
  -p, --port <PORT>          TCP port to listen on [env: PORT] [default: 3456]
  -d, --db <PATH>            Local commonmeta SQLite3 database [env: COMMONMETA_DB]
      --pid-file <PATH>      Write PID to this file on startup [env: DRAGOMAN_PID_FILE]
dragoman stop [OPTIONS]
      --pid-file <PATH>      PID file to read [env: DRAGOMAN_PID_FILE] [default: /tmp/dragoman.pid]
```
## Environment variables

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `PORT` | `3456` | TCP port to listen on. |
| `COMMONMETA_DB` | (platform default) | Path to a local commonmeta SQLite3 database. Metadata is served from the database before falling back to the live API. If the file does not exist, a warning is logged and the server starts without a local database. Platform defaults: macOS → `~/Library/Application Support/commonmeta/commonmeta.sqlite3`; Linux →`/var/lib/commonmeta/commonmeta.sqlite3`. |
| `DRAGOMAN_PID_FILE` | (none) | Path for the PID file written by `start`and read by`stop`. |
| `RUST_LOG` | `dragoman=info` | Log filter (see ). Use`tracing-subscriber``dragoman=debug`to log per-request cache hits. |

#### Formatted citation

`text/x-bibliography` accepts optional `style=` and `locale=` parameters. Style names come from the [CSL style repository](https://github.com/citation-style-language/styles); locale codes from the [CSL locales repository](https://github.com/citation-style-language/locales).

```

```

### Format-specific URL prefixes

Two URL prefixes return a fixed format without requiring an `Accept` header or `?format=` parameter:

| Prefix | Output format | Content-Type |
|---|---|---|
| `/dois/{doi}` | DataCite JSON | `application/vnd.datacite.datacite+json` |
| `/works/{doi}` | Crossref JSON | `application/vnd.crossref+json` |

```
```
These routes are equivalent to `/{doi}?format=datacite` and `/{doi}?format=crossref` respectively. The `?source=` override is still accepted if you need to force a specific registration agency.

## Supported formats

| Accept header | `?format=`value | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `application/x-bibtex` | `bibtex` | |
| `text/x-bibliography` | `citation` | `style=`and`locale=`params |
| `application/vnd.commonmeta+json` | `commonmeta` | |
| `application/vnd.crossref+json` | `crossref` | |
| `application/vnd.crossref.unixref+xml` | `crossref_xml` | |
| `application/vnd.crossref.unixsd+xml` | `crossref_xml` | alias |
| `application/vnd.citationstyles.csl+json` | `csl` | |
| `application/vnd.datacite.datacite+json` | `datacite` | |
| `application/vnd.datacite.datacite+xml` | `datacite_xml` | |
| `application/vnd.inveniordm.v1+json` | `inveniordm` | |
| `application/x-research-info-systems` | `ris` | |
| `application/vnd.schemaorg.ld+json` | `schemaorg` | |
| `text/html`/(absent) | — | 307 redirect to landing page |

## HTTP status codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 200 | Metadata returned |
| 307 | Redirect to landing page |
| 404 | DOI not found |
| 406 | Requested content type not supported |
| 502 | Upstream API error |

## Deployment (macOS)

### Installation via Homebrew

dragoman can be installed from the [front-matter Homebrew tap](https://github.com/front-matter/homebrew-tap):

```
```
This builds dragoman from source (requires Rust, installed automatically as a build dependency) and places the binary at `$(brew --prefix)/bin/dragoman`.

#### Place the database

The platform default path on macOS is `~/Library/Application Support/commonmeta/commonmeta.sqlite3`. Place the database there and no further configuration is needed:

```
```
To use a different path, set `COMMONMETA_DB` in the launchd plist or pass `--db` on the command line.

#### Run as a background service (launchd)

```
# Start at login and keep alive
# Check status
# View logs
# Stop the service
```
`brew services start` installs a launchd plist in `~/Library/LaunchAgents/` and starts the service immediately. It restarts automatically on crash and at login.

To run as a system-level daemon (starts at boot, not tied to a user login), use `sudo brew services start dragoman`. This installs the plist in `/Library/LaunchDaemons/` instead.

#### Configuration

To change the port or other settings, edit the service environment variables and restart:

```
# Open the generated plist for editing
```

### Updating the database

The database file can be replaced while the service is running without restarting. dragoman opens a new read-only SQLite connection per request, so an atomic rename takes effect immediately for new requests while in-flight requests finish against the old file.

Copy the new file to a staging path on the same filesystem, then rename it over the live file:

```
```
If the source database uses WAL mode (has accompanying `-wal`/`-shm` files), produce a clean single-file snapshot first with `VACUUM INTO` before copying:

```
```

```
```

When`update`is false the output file is deleted and recreated (default). When`update`is true the existing file is kept and rows are upserted by their`id`primary key — new rows are inserted, existing rows are replaced. Returns the number of records written. No`Vec<Data>`is held for the whole file — peak memory is proportional to one batch, not the whole dump.

# krishiv_plan - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-plan/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_plan/

## Expand description

Logical and physical plan types for Krishiv.

R1 bootstrap keeps these types deliberately small. Later R1 work will bridge them to DataFusion logical and physical plans without exposing DataFusion as the long-term public Krishiv API.

# krishiv_engine_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-engine-core/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_engine_core/

## Expand description

Krishiv engine-core: the three-engine spine.

Krishiv runs **three distinct compute engines** that share one execution
contract:

- `EngineKind::Batch`
- `EngineKind::Incremental`
- `EngineKind::Streaming`

The **engine** (compute model), the **placement** (embedded / single-node /
distributed), and the **API surface** (SQL / Python / Rust) are three
independent axes. Every front-end compiles to a single [ CompiledJob](https://docs.rs/struct.CompiledJob.html); a

[runs it using placement-provided services carried by](https://docs.rs/trait.ComputeEngine.html)

`ComputeEngine`[. The same engine code therefore runs unchanged from an embedded in-process call to a distributed cluster — only the injected services differ.](https://docs.rs/struct.EngineRuntime.html)

`EngineRuntime`This crate is the bottom of the engine stack: it depends only on
`krishiv-common`, `krishiv-proto`, and Arrow, so every engine and front-end
crate can depend on it without a cycle.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use consolidate::`- [ConsolidatingSinkProvider](https://docs.rs/consolidate/struct.ConsolidatingSinkProvider.html);
- `pub use durable::`- [DurableCheckpointService](https://docs.rs/durable/struct.DurableCheckpointService.html);
- `pub use upsert::`- [UpsertSinkProvider](https://docs.rs/upsert/struct.UpsertSinkProvider.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

# krishiv_delta - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-delta/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_delta/

## Expand description

`krishiv-delta` — Incremental computing engine for Krishiv.

This crate implements the algebraic incremental view maintenance layer inspired by Feldera/DBSP (Z-set bilinear operators, Spine-style Trace) and CocoIndex (behavior versioning, convergent roll-forward commit, tiered change detection).

[§](https://docs.rs#core-concepts)Core Concepts

-
`DeltaBatch``RecordBatch`where each row has an`i64`weight:`+1`= insertion,`-1`= retraction,`0`= cancelled.
-
`Trace``DeltaBatch`es across ticks. Used by stateful operators (join, aggregate) to probe historical state efficiently.
-
`LogicFingerprint``(operator_uid, behavior_version)`. When bumped, it signals that an operator’s logic has changed and its cached Trace state should be discarded and recomputed.
-
`WatermarkTracker``max_ts - lateness_ms`are dropped; Trace entries below the watermark are eligible for GC.
-
`CoalescingMap`

[§](https://docs.rs#operator-library)Operator library

| Operator | Module | Kind |
|---|---|---|
| map / project | `operators::map` | Linear (no state) |
| filter | `operators::filter` | Linear (no state) |
| consolidate | `operators::consolidate` | Linear (no state) |
| join | `operators::join` | Bilinear (two Traces) |
| aggregate | `operators::aggregate` | Nonlinear (running state) |
| distinct | `operators::distinct` | Nonlinear (count map) |
| recursive | `operators::recursive` | Fixed-point loop |

# agent-team-mail (`atm`)

`agent-team-mail` is the retained `1.0` CLI and core library for local ATM
mailbox workflows.

This repository is now the source of truth for publishing:

- `agent-team-mail`
- `agent-team-mail-core`

The installed command remains `atm`.

## What `1.0` Includes

The retained `1.0` release scope is the daemon-free CLI/core pair:

- `agent-team-mail`— the- `atm`CLI
- `agent-team-mail-core`— the core Rust library used by the CLI

This release line continues to consume the published `sc-observability` family
for retained logging and health reporting:

- `sc-observability-types`
- `sc-observability-otlp`

This repo does not publish the retired legacy daemon, MCP, TUI, or CI-monitor
artifacts as part of the retained `1.0` surface.

## Post-Send Hook

`atm send` can run an optional post-send hook configured in `.atm.toml`:

```
[[]]
 = "team-lead"
 = ["scripts/atm-nudge.sh", "team-lead"]
[[]]
 = "arch-ctm"
 = ["scripts/atm-nudge.sh", "arch-ctm"]
```
Behavior:

- Each `[[atm.post_send_hooks]]`rule binds one`recipient`and one`command`.
- `recipient`matches either one exact member name or- `*`for all recipients.
- Multiple matching rules all run, in config order.
- If `command[0]`is path-like, ATM resolves it relative to the directory containing`.atm.toml`.
- Bare executables like `bash`,`python3`, or`tmux`use normal`PATH`resolution.
- Recipient non-match is silent.
- ATM rejects retired `post_send_hook`,`post_send_hook_senders`,`post_send_hook_recipients`, and`post_send_hook_members`keys with migration guidance.
- ATM sets `ATM_POST_SEND`to a JSON payload with`{from, to, sender, recipient, team, message_id, requires_ack}`plus optional`task_id`when present.
- The hook gets 5 seconds to complete.
- Hook stderr is suppressed. Hook stdout may optionally return one JSON object with `level`,`message`, and optional`fields`for ATM to log.
- For troubleshooting hook diagnostics, combine `--stderr-logs`with`ATM_LOG=debug`to surface debug-level hook results on stderr.
- If the hook exits non-zero, fails to start, or times out, `atm send`still succeeds and prints a warning.

Example `ATM_POST_SEND` payload:

```
```
Example tmux auto-nudge hook for a Codex pane:

```
#!/usr/bin/env bash
recipient=""
team=""
```
Optional structured hook result on stdout:

```
```

# sim_kernel - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-kernel/^0.1.0-rc.1/

## Expand description

sim-kernel is the small protocol kernel of the SIM Rust runtime.

The kernel defines contracts; libraries supply behavior. This crate holds
the protocol and contract types – forms, values, stores, registry and
callable surfaces, the [ shape](https://docs.rs/shape/index.html) protocol, evaluation policy, and the ABI
transport – while concrete behavior (parsers, number domains, the standard
distribution, and server/agent/browse implementations) lives in separate
library crates loaded against these contracts. SIM is a Rust runtime, not a
Lisp runtime; Lisp is one codec surface among several.

The one deliberate exception is the pair of built-in *reference backends*:
[ list::VecList](https://docs.rs/list/struct.VecList.html) (a

[) and](https://docs.rs/list/trait.ListValue.html)

`list::ListValue`[(a](https://docs.rs/table/struct.AssocTable.html)

`table::AssocTable`[). These are the kernel’s bootstrap list and table implementations – minimal, correct, and self-annotated](https://docs.rs/table/trait.Table.html)

`table::Table``sim-non-citizen` –
so the runtime can stand up collections before any library loads. They are
reference implementations, not the only backends: alternatives load as libs
against the [/](https://docs.rs/list/trait.ListBackend.html)

`list::ListBackend`[contracts. (Future cleanup: move even these into a default-loaded distribution lib so the kernel ships pure contracts; tracked against the constellation reorg.)](https://docs.rs/table/trait.TableBackend.html)

`table::TableBackend`The kernel data flow is:

`tokens -> checked forms -> objects -> checked calls -> objects -> encoded forms`[§](https://docs.rs#module-map)Module map

Core forms and values: [ value](https://docs.rs/value/index.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/expr/index.html)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [callable](https://docs.rs/callable/index.html)
- The callable contract: objects that can be invoked with checked arguments.

- Capability names and sets: the contract for gating privileged operations.
- [card](https://docs.rs/card/index.html)
- Card records: the contract for structured metadata about runtime subjects.
- [catalog](https://docs.rs/catalog/index.html)
- The registry catalog substrate: transactional, `Cx`-free table storage.
- [claim](https://docs.rs/claim/index.html)
- Claims: the contract for asserted facts about runtime subjects.

- The class contract: callable factories with subclass relationships.

- Control policy: the contract for delimited prompts, capture, and resume.

# sim_lib_control - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-control/^0.1.0-rc.1/

## Expand description

Control behavior for the SIM runtime: async, backtracking, conditions.

The kernel defines the control-policy contracts; this crate supplies the concrete control organ (coroutines, generators, restarts, non-local exits) layered over those contracts.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Async](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncTask.html)- Task
- A deterministic async task that resolves after a fixed number of polls.
- [Backtracker](https://docs.rs/struct.Backtracker.html)
- A linear backtracking choice point over a fixed list of alternatives.
- [Condition](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html)
- A signalled condition: a kind symbol plus a payload reference.
- [Condition](https://docs.rs/struct.ConditionHandler.html)- Handler
- A handler bound to a condition kind, prompt, and capture continuation.
- [Condition](https://docs.rs/struct.ConditionStack.html)- Stack
- A stack of `ConditionHandler`
- [Continuation](https://docs.rs/struct.ContinuationValue.html)- Value
- A runtime object wrapping a captured continuation and its capture result.
- [Control](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlFunction.html)- Function
- A callable runtime object exposing one control primitive.
- [Control](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlLib.html)- Lib
- The control organ as a loadable kernel `Lib`
- [Control](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlResultValue.html)- Result - Value
- A runtime object wrapping the result reference of a control operation.
- [Control](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlTag.html)- Tag
- Stable tag identifying a delimited control prompt.
- [Coroutine](https://docs.rs/struct.Coroutine.html)
- Two cooperating value streams that yield by alternating between lanes.
- [Generator](https://docs.rs/struct.Generator.html)
- A single-lane generator that yields a fixed sequence of values on demand.
- [Labeled](https://docs.rs/struct.LabeledPrompt.html)- Prompt
- A labeled escape target: a label symbol bound to a control prompt.
- [NonLocal](https://docs.rs/struct.NonLocalExit.html)- Exit
- A pending non-local exit: a kind, a target label, and a carried value.
- [OneShot](https://docs.rs/struct.OneShotControlPolicy.html)- Control - Policy
- A control policy that allows each captured continuation to resume once.
- [Restart](https://docs.rs/struct.Restart.html)
- A named recovery point: a symbol bound to a captured continuation.
- [Restart](https://docs.rs/struct.RestartStack.html)- Stack
- A stack of `Restart`
- [Segmented](https://docs.rs/struct.SegmentedControlPolicy.html)- Control - Policy
- A one-shot control policy scoped to a named delimited segment.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Async](https://docs.rs/enum.AsyncPoll.html)- Poll
- Outcome of polling an `AsyncTask`
- [Backtrack](https://docs.rs/enum.BacktrackStep.html)- Step
- Result of advancing a `Backtracker`
- [Coroutine](https://docs.rs/enum.CoroutineLane.html)- Lane
- Identifies which of a coroutine’s two cooperating lanes yielded a value.
- [Coroutine](https://docs.rs/enum.CoroutineStep.html)- Step
- Outcome of resuming a `Coroutine`
- [Generator](https://docs.rs/enum.GeneratorStep.html)- Step
- Outcome of advancing a `Generator`
- [NonLocal](https://docs.rs/enum.NonLocalExitKind.html)- Exit - Kind
- The flavor of a non-local exit: loop break, loop continue, or block return.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Control](https://docs.rs/trait.ControlPrompt.html)- Prompt
- Library-level contract for prompts raised by runtime organs.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [abort_](https://docs.rs/fn.abort_symbol.html)- symbol
- Returns the `control/abort`symbol.
- [capture_](https://docs.rs/fn.capture_symbol.html)- symbol
- Returns the `control/capture`symbol.
- [control_](https://docs.rs/fn.control_exports.html)- exports
- Returns the lib’s exported `control/*`functions as kernel`Export`
- [control_](https://docs.rs/fn.control_op_keys.html)- op_ - keys
- Returns the standard control operation keys this organ claims:
`prompt`,`capture`,`abort`, and`resume`.
- [control_](https://docs.rs/fn.control_organ_symbol.html)- organ_ - symbol
- Returns the `organ/control`symbol identifying this control organ.
- [escape_](https://docs.rs/fn.escape_to_label.html)- to_ - label
- Performs `exit`by aborting to the matching`LabeledPrompt``prompts`.
- [install_](https://docs.rs/fn.install_control_lib.html)- control_ - lib
- Installs the control organ into `cx`: loads`ControlLib`
- [install_](https://docs.rs/fn.install_control_policy.html)- control_ - policy
- Installs the default `one_shot_control_policy``cx`as the active control policy.
- [invoke_](https://docs.rs/fn.invoke_restart.html)- restart
- Invokes the restart named `name`on`stack`with`value`; free-function form of`RestartStack::invoke`
- [manifest_](https://docs.rs/fn.manifest_name.html)- name
- Returns the `sim/control`manifest id under which this lib registers.
- [one_](https://docs.rs/fn.one_shot_control_policy.html)- shot_ - control_ - policy
- Builds a shared `OneShotControlPolicy``ControlPolicyRef`
- [prompt_](https://docs.rs/fn.prompt_symbol.html)- symbol
- Returns the `control/prompt`symbol.
- [publish_](https://docs.rs/fn.publish_control_organ_claims.html)- control_ - organ_ - claims
- Publishes the control organ’s claims into `cx`, recording that this organ supplies the standard`control_op_keys``control_organ_symbol`
- [publish_](https://docs.rs/fn.publish_control_organ_claims_for_lib.html)- control_ - organ_ - claims_ - for_ - lib
- Publishes control organ claims as part of a loaded lib receipt.
- [raise_](https://docs.rs/fn.raise_prompt.html)- prompt
- Raises a library-level control prompt through the kernel control contract.
- [resume_](https://docs.rs/fn.resume_symbol.html)- symbol
- Returns the `control/resume`symbol.
- [segmented_](https://docs.rs/fn.segmented_control_policy.html)- control_ - policy
- Builds a shared `SegmentedControlPolicy``segment`as a kernel`ControlPolicyRef`
- [signal_](https://docs.rs/fn.signal_condition.html)- condition
- Signals `condition`against`stack`; free-function form of`ConditionStack::signal`

# sim_lib_dispatch - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-dispatch/^0.1.0-rc.1/

## Expand description

Generic functions and method dispatch for the SIM runtime.

The kernel defines the callable and operation contracts; this crate supplies the concrete dispatch organ (generic functions, multimethods, method specificity ordering).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Dispatch](https://docs.rs/struct.DispatchMethod.html)- Method
- A single method belonging to a `GenericFunction`
- [Generic](https://docs.rs/struct.GenericFunction.html)- Function
- A named generic function: a set of `DispatchMethod`
- [Method](https://docs.rs/struct.MethodSpecificity.html)- Specificity
- How specifically a method matched a particular call.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Method](https://docs.rs/enum.MethodRole.html)- Role
- Role of a method within a generic function’s combination.

## Statics[§](https://docs.rs#statics)

- [RECIPES](https://docs.rs/static.RECIPES.html)
- Cookbook recipes for the dispatch organ, embedded at build time.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [compare_](https://docs.rs/fn.compare_specificity.html)- specificity
- Orders two specificities from least to most specific.
- [dispatch_](https://docs.rs/fn.dispatch_combine_op_key.html)- combine_ - op_ - key
- Operation key for method combination (around/before/primary/after).
- [dispatch_](https://docs.rs/fn.dispatch_generic_op_key.html)- generic_ - op_ - key
- Operation key for defining a generic function.
- [dispatch_](https://docs.rs/fn.dispatch_inspect_op_key.html)- inspect_ - op_ - key
- Operation key for inspecting the applicable methods of a call.
- [dispatch_](https://docs.rs/fn.dispatch_multimethod_op_key.html)- multimethod_ - op_ - key
- Operation key for adding a method to a generic function (multimethod).
- [dispatch_](https://docs.rs/fn.dispatch_op_keys.html)- op_ - keys
- All operation keys contributed by the dispatch organ, in claim order.
- [dispatch_](https://docs.rs/fn.dispatch_organ_symbol.html)- organ_ - symbol
- Symbol identifying the dispatch organ in the claim store.
- [dispatch_](https://docs.rs/fn.dispatch_specificity_op_key.html)- specificity_ - op_ - key
- Operation key for reporting method specificity for a call.
- [publish_](https://docs.rs/fn.publish_dispatch_organ_claims.html)- dispatch_ - organ_ - claims
- Publishes the dispatch organ’s claims and operation keys into a `Cx`
- [publish_](https://docs.rs/fn.publish_dispatch_organ_claims_for_lib.html)- dispatch_ - organ_ - claims_ - for_ - lib
- Publishes dispatch organ claims as part of a loaded lib receipt.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Method](https://docs.rs/type.MethodBody.html)- Body
- The executable body of a `DispatchMethod`
- [Multimethod](https://docs.rs/type.Multimethod.html)
- A generic function under its multimethod alias.

# sim_lib_standard_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-standard-core/^0.1.0-rc.1/

## Expand description

Standard distribution core for the SIM runtime.

The kernel defines the capability, claim, codec, and `ExportRecord`
contracts; this crate supplies the standard-distribution behavior:
capabilities, claims, diff, fidelity, the conformance harness, install,
language-profile support, the lisp codec surface, polyglot/profile support,
and read/construct.

# sim_lib_lang_ruby - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sim-lib-lang-ruby/0.1.0-rc.1/target-redirect/sim_lib_lang_ruby/

## Expand description

Ruby DSL surface profile for the SIM runtime.

The kernel defines the codec, eval-policy, and `Expr` contracts; this crate
is a loadable language profile presenting a Ruby surface syntax over the
shared `Expr` graph, not a standalone interpreter.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Ruby](https://docs.rs/struct.RubyBlockScope.html)- Block - Scope
- A labeled Ruby block scope targeted by `break`and`next`exits.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [install_](https://docs.rs/fn.install_ruby_dsl_profile.html)- ruby_ - dsl_ - profile
- Installs the Ruby DSL profile and its organ claims into a registry.
- [ruby_](https://docs.rs/fn.ruby_blocks_fidelity_symbol.html)- blocks_ - fidelity_ - symbol
- Stable symbol for the Ruby full-blocks fidelity badge (limited support).
- [ruby_](https://docs.rs/fn.ruby_break.html)- break
- Performs a Ruby `break`, escaping the block scope with`value`.
- [ruby_](https://docs.rs/fn.ruby_conformance_test_symbol.html)- conformance_ - test_ - symbol
- Stable symbol for the Ruby DSL control conformance test.
- [ruby_](https://docs.rs/fn.ruby_control_fidelity_symbol.html)- control_ - fidelity_ - symbol
- Stable symbol for the Ruby control-blocks fidelity badge.
- [ruby_](https://docs.rs/fn.ruby_dispatch_fidelity_symbol.html)- dispatch_ - fidelity_ - symbol
- Stable symbol for the Ruby method-dispatch fidelity badge.
- [ruby_](https://docs.rs/fn.ruby_dsl_matrix_row.html)- dsl_ - matrix_ - row
- Builds the Ruby DSL matrix row.
- [ruby_](https://docs.rs/fn.ruby_dsl_profile.html)- dsl_ - profile
- Builds the `LanguageProfile`
- [ruby_](https://docs.rs/fn.ruby_dsl_source_cases.html)- dsl_ - source_ - cases
- Minimal source cases for the Ruby DSL matrix row.
- [ruby_](https://docs.rs/fn.ruby_lowering_symbol.html)- lowering_ - symbol
- Stable symbol for the Ruby lowering from surface forms to `Expr`.
- [ruby_](https://docs.rs/fn.ruby_next.html)- next
- Performs a Ruby `next`, advancing the block scope with`value`.
- [ruby_](https://docs.rs/fn.ruby_profile_symbol.html)- profile_ - symbol
- Stable symbol identifying the Ruby DSL language profile.
- [ruby_](https://docs.rs/fn.ruby_reader_symbol.html)- reader_ - symbol
- Stable symbol for the reader codec the Ruby surface decodes through.
- [run_](https://docs.rs/fn.run_ruby_dsl_conformance_case.html)- ruby_ - dsl_ - conformance_ - case
- Runs one Ruby DSL source conformance case.
- [run_](https://docs.rs/fn.run_ruby_dsl_matrix_row.html)- ruby_ - dsl_ - matrix_ - row
- Runs the Ruby DSL matrix row and publishes claim-backed cells.

# RubyBlockScope in sim_lib_lang_ruby - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-lang-ruby/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_lang_ruby/struct.RubyBlockScope.html

`pub struct RubyBlockScope { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A labeled Ruby block scope targeted by `break` and `next` exits.

Lowers Ruby block control onto the control organ’s labeled-prompt contract: the scope pairs a label with the control prompt that bounds it.

# install_ruby_dsl_profile in sim_lib_lang_ruby - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-lang-ruby/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_lang_ruby/fn.install_ruby_dsl_profile.html

```
pub fn install_ruby_dsl_profile(
    cx: &mut
```
[Cx](https://docs.rs/sim-kernel/0.1.0-rc.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sim_kernel/env/core/struct.Cx.html),
    registry: &mut [ProfileRegistry](https://docs.rs/sim-lib-standard-core/0.1.0-rc.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sim_lib_standard_core/registry/struct.ProfileRegistry.html),
) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/sim-kernel/0.1.0-rc.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sim_kernel/error/type.Result.html)<[LanguageProfile](https://docs.rs/sim-lib-standard-core/0.1.0-rc.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sim_lib_standard_core/profile/struct.LanguageProfile.html)>## Expand description

Installs the Ruby DSL profile and its organ claims into a registry.

First-reach entry point: registers [ ruby_dsl_profile](https://docs.rs/fn.ruby_dsl_profile.html) through the standard
profile installer, publishing the control- and dispatch-organ claims so the
surface becomes loadable.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use std::sync::Arc;
use sim_kernel::{Cx, DefaultFactory, NoopEvalPolicy, Symbol};
use sim_lib_standard_core::ProfileRegistry;
use sim_lib_lang_ruby::install_ruby_dsl_profile;
let mut cx = Cx::new(Arc::new(NoopEvalPolicy), Arc::new(DefaultFactory));
let mut registry = ProfileRegistry::new();
let profile = install_ruby_dsl_profile(&mut cx, &mut registry).unwrap();
assert_eq!(profile.reader, Symbol::qualified("codec", "algol"));
```

# ruby_dsl_profile in sim_lib_lang_ruby - Rust

`pub fn ruby_dsl_profile() -> `[LanguageProfile](https://docs.rs/sim-lib-standard-core/0.1.0-rc.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sim_lib_standard_core/profile/struct.LanguageProfile.html)## Expand description

Builds the [ LanguageProfile](https://docs.rs/sim-lib-standard-core/0.1.0-rc.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sim_lib_standard_core/profile/struct.LanguageProfile.html) describing the Ruby DSL surface profile.

pub struct LanguageProfile {
    pub symbol:

    pub eval_policy: [Symbol](https://docs.rs/sim-kernel/0.1.0-rc.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sim_kernel/id/struct.Symbol.html),
    pub organs: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[OrganUse](https://docs.rs/struct.OrganUse.html)>,
    pub numeric_tower: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Symbol](https://docs.rs/sim-kernel/0.1.0-rc.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sim_kernel/id/struct.Symbol.html)>,
    pub capabilities: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[CapabilityName](https://docs.rs/sim-kernel/0.1.0-rc.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sim_kernel/capability/struct.CapabilityName.html)>,
    pub unsupported_forms: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[Symbol](https://docs.rs/sim-kernel/0.1.0-rc.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sim_kernel/id/struct.Symbol.html)>,
    pub conformance_tests: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[Symbol](https://docs.rs/sim-kernel/0.1.0-rc.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sim_kernel/id/struct.Symbol.html)>,
    pub fidelity_badges: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[FidelityBadge](https://docs.rs/fidelity/struct.FidelityBadge.html)>,
}## Expand description

A language profile: the reader, lowering, eval-policy, organs, and metadata
that present one surface language over the shared `Expr` graph.

Profiles are the unit the standard distribution installs, diffs, and tests;
the per-language `sim-lib-lang-*` crates build one each.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use sim_kernel::Symbol;
use sim_lib_standard_core::{LanguageProfile, OrganUse, standard_control_organ_symbol};
let profile = LanguageProfile::new(Symbol::qualified("lang", "demo/v1"))
    .with_reader(Symbol::qualified("codec", "lisp"))
    .with_eval_policy(Symbol::qualified("eval", "default"))
    .with_organ(OrganUse::new(standard_control_organ_symbol()));
assert_eq!(profile.reader, Symbol::qualified("codec", "lisp"));
assert_eq!(profile.organs.len(), 1);
```

# arrow - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/arrow/^58.3.0/

## Expand description

A complete, safe, native Rust implementation of [Apache Arrow](https://arrow.apache.org), a cross-language
development platform for in-memory data.

Please see the [arrow crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/arrow)
page for feature flags and tips to improve performance.

[§](https://docs.rs#columnar-format)Columnar Format

The [ array](https://docs.rs/array/index.html) module provides statically typed implementations of all the array types as defined
by the

[Arrow Columnar Format](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/Columnar.html)

For example, an [ Int32Array](https://docs.rs/array/type.Int32Array.html) represents a nullable array of

`i32````
let array = Int32Array::from(vec![Some(1), None, Some(3)]);
assert_eq!(array.len(), 3);
assert_eq!(array.value(0), 1);
assert_eq!(array.is_null(1), true);
let collected: Vec<_> = array.iter().collect();
assert_eq!(collected, vec![Some(1), None, Some(3)]);
assert_eq!(array.values(), &[1, 0, 3])
```
It is also possible to write generic code for different concrete types. For example, since the following function is generic over all primitively typed arrays, when invoked the Rust compiler will generate specialized implementations with optimized code for each concrete type.

```
fn sum<T: ArrowPrimitiveType>(array: &PrimitiveArray<T>) -> T::Native
where
    T: ArrowPrimitiveType,
    T::Native: Sum
{
    array.iter().map(|v| v.unwrap_or_default()).sum()
}
assert_eq!(sum(&Float32Array::from(vec![1.1, 2.9, 3.])), 7.);
assert_eq!(sum(&TimestampNanosecondArray::from(vec![1, 2, 3])), 6);
```
And the following uses [ ArrayAccessor](https://docs.rs/array/trait.ArrayAccessor.html) to implement a generic function
over all arrays with comparable values.

```
fn min<T: ArrayAccessor>(array: T) -> Option<T::Item>
where
    T::Item: Ord
{
    ArrayIter::new(array).filter_map(|v| v).min()
}
assert_eq!(min(&Int32Array::from(vec![4, 2, 1, 6])), Some(1));
assert_eq!(min(&StringArray::from(vec!["b", "a", "c"])), Some("a"));
```
**For more examples, and details consult the  arrow_array docs.**

[§](https://docs.rs#type-erasure--trait-objects)Type Erasure / Trait Objects

It is common to write code that handles any type of array, without necessarily
knowing its concrete type. This is done using the [ Array](https://docs.rs/array/index.html) trait and using

[to determine the appropriate](https://docs.rs/datatypes/enum.DataType.html)

`DataType``downcast_ref`.```
fn impl_string(array: &StringArray) {}
fn impl_f32(array: &Float32Array) {}
fn impl_dyn(array: &dyn Array) {
    match array.data_type() {
        // downcast `dyn Array` to concrete `StringArray`
        DataType::Utf8 => impl_string(array.as_any().downcast_ref().unwrap()),
        // downcast `dyn Array` to concrete `Float32Array`
        DataType::Float32 => impl_f32(array.as_any().downcast_ref().unwrap()),
        _ => unimplemented!()
    }
}
```
You can use the [ AsArray](https://docs.rs/array/trait.AsArray.html) extension trait to facilitate downcasting:

```
fn impl_string(array: &StringArray) {}
fn impl_f32(array: &Float32Array) {}
fn impl_dyn(array: &dyn Array) {
    match array.data_type() {
        DataType::Utf8 => impl_string(array.as_string()),
        DataType::Float32 => impl_f32(array.as_primitive()),
        _ => unimplemented!()
    }
}
```
It is also common to want to write a function that returns one of a number of possible
array implementations. [ ArrayRef](https://docs.rs/array/type.ArrayRef.html) is a type-alias for

[which is frequently used for this purpose](https://docs.rs/array/trait.Array.html)

`Arc<dyn Array>````
fn parse_to_primitive<'a, T, I>(iter: I) -> PrimitiveArray<T>
where
    T: ArrowPrimitiveType,
    T::Native: FromStr,
    I: IntoIterator<Item=&'a str>,
{
    PrimitiveArray::from_iter(iter.into_iter().map(|val| T::Native::from_str(val).ok()))
}
fn parse_strings<'a, I>(iter: I, to_data_type: DataType) -> ArrayRef
where
    I: IntoIterator<Item=&'a str>,
{
   match to_data_type {
       DataType::Int32 => Arc::new(parse_to_primitive::<Int32Type, _>(iter)) as _,
       DataType::UInt32 => Arc::new(parse_to_primitive::<UInt32Type, _>(iter)) as _,
       _ => unimplemented!()
   }
}
let array = parse_strings(["1", "2", "3"], DataType::Int32);
let integers = array.as_any().downcast_ref::<Int32Array>().unwrap();
assert_eq!(integers.values(), &[1, 2, 3])
```
[§](https://docs.rs#compute-kernels)Compute Kernels

The [ compute](https://docs.rs/compute/index.html) module provides optimised implementations of many common operations,
for example the

`parse_strings` operation above could also be implemented as follows:```
fn parse_strings<'a, I>(iter: I, to_data_type: &DataType) -> Result<ArrayRef>
where
    I: IntoIterator<Item=&'a str>,
{
    let array = StringArray::from_iter(iter.into_iter().map(Some));
    arrow::compute::cast(&array, to_data_type)
}
let array = parse_strings(["1", "2", "3"], &DataType::UInt32).unwrap();
let integers = array.as_any().downcast_ref::<UInt32Array>().unwrap();
assert_eq!(integers.values(), &[1, 2, 3])
```
This module also implements many common vertical operations:

- All mathematical binary operators, such as `sub`
- All boolean binary operators such as `equality`
- `cast`
- `filter`
- `take`
- `sort`
- some string operators such as `substring``length`

```
let array = Int32Array::from_iter(0..100);
// Create a 32-bit integer scalar (single) value:
let scalar = Int32Array::new_scalar(60);
// find all rows in the array that are greater than 60
let predicate = gt(&array, &scalar).unwrap();
// copy all matching rows into a new array
let filtered = filter(&array, &predicate).unwrap();
let expected = Int32Array::from_iter(61..100);
assert_eq!(&expected, filtered.as_primitive::<Int32Type>());
```
As well as some horizontal operations, such as:

[§](https://docs.rs#tabular-representation)Tabular Representation

It is common to want to group one or more columns together into a tabular representation. This
is provided by [ RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/array/struct.RecordBatch.html) which combines a

[and a corresponding list of](https://docs.rs/datatypes/struct.Schema.html)

`Schema`[.](https://docs.rs/array/type.ArrayRef.html)

`ArrayRef````
let col_1 = Arc::new(Int32Array::from_iter([1, 2, 3])) as _;
let col_2 = Arc::new(Float32Array::from_iter([1., 6.3, 4.])) as _;
let batch = RecordBatch::try_from_iter([("col1", col_1), ("col_2", col_2)]).unwrap();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#pretty-printing)Pretty Printing

See the [ util::pretty](https://docs.rs/util/pretty/index.html) module (requires the

`prettyprint` crate feature)[§](https://docs.rs#io)IO

This crate provides readers and writers for various formats to/from `RecordBatch`

Support for [Apache Parquet](https://parquet.apache.org/) is published as a [separate parquet crate](https://crates.io/crates/parquet)

Support for [Apache Avro](https://avro.apache.org/) is published as a [separate arrow-avro crate](https://crates.io/crates/arrow-avro)

[§](https://docs.rs#serde-compatibility)Serde Compatibility

[ arrow_json::reader::Decoder](https://docs.rs/arrow-json/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_json/reader/struct.Decoder.html) provides a mechanism to convert arbitrary, serde-compatible
structures into

[.](https://docs.rs/array/struct.RecordBatch.html)

`RecordBatch`Whilst likely less performant than implementing a custom builder, as described in
[arrow_array::builder](https://docs.rs/array/builder/index.html), this provides a simple mechanism to get up and running quickly

```
#[derive(Serialize)]
struct MyStruct {
    int32: i32,
    string: String,
}
let schema = Schema::new(vec![
    Field::new("int32", DataType::Int32, false),
    Field::new("string", DataType::Utf8, false),
]);
let rows = vec![
    MyStruct{ int32: 5, string: "bar".to_string() },
    MyStruct{ int32: 8, string: "foo".to_string() },
];
let mut decoder = ReaderBuilder::new(Arc::new(schema)).build_decoder().unwrap();
decoder.serialize(&rows).unwrap();
let batch = decoder.flush().unwrap().unwrap();
// Expect batch containing two columns
let int32 = batch.column(0).as_primitive::<Int32Type>();
assert_eq!(int32.values(), &[5, 8]);
let string = batch.column(1).as_string::<i32>();
assert_eq!(string.value(0), "bar");
assert_eq!(string.value(1), "foo");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#crate-topology)Crate Topology

The [ arrow](https://github.com/apache/arrow-rs) project is implemented as multiple sub-crates, which are then re-exported by
this top-level crate.

Crate authors can choose to depend on this top-level crate, or just the sub-crates they need.

The current list of sub-crates is:

Some functionality is also distributed independently of this crate:

- `parquet`- [Apache Parquet](https://parquet.apache.org/)

[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

This project follows the [Apache Arrow Security Model](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/dev/format/Security.html).

Unexpected behavior (e.g., panics, crashes, or infinite loops) triggered by
malformed input is considered a **bug**, not a security vulnerability,
unless it is **exploitable** by an attacker to

- Execute arbitrary code (Remote Code Execution);
- Exfiltrate sensitive information from process memory (Information Disclosure);

If you think you have found a security vulnerability, please follow the
reporting instructions in the [security policy](https://github.com/apache/arrow-rs/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

Like many crates, this crate makes use of `unsafe` where prudent. However, it endeavors to be
sound. Specifically, **it should not be possible to trigger undefined behavior using safe APIs.**

Undefined behavior using safe APIs is considered a bug, not a security
vulnerability, unless it can be exploited. Please see the [security policy](https://github.com/apache/arrow-rs/blob/main/SECURITY.md)
for details.

For more information on the use of `unsafe`, see [here](https://github.com/apache/arrow-rs/tree/main/arrow#safety).

[§](https://docs.rs#higher-level-processing)Higher-level Processing

This crate aims to provide reusable, low-level primitives for operating on columnar data. For
more sophisticated query processing workloads, consider checking out [DataFusion](https://github.com/apache/arrow-datafusion). This
orchestrates the primitives exported by this crate into an embeddable query engine, with
SQL and DataFrame frontends, and heavily influences this crate’s roadmap.

# askama - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/askama/^0.16.0/

## Expand description

Askama implements a type-safe compiler for Jinja-like templates.
It lets you write templates in a Jinja-like syntax,
which are linked to a `struct` or an `enum` defining the template context.
This is done using a custom derive implementation (implemented
in [ askama_macros](https://crates.io/crates/askama_macros)).

For feature highlights and a quick start, please review the
[README](https://github.com/askama-rs/askama/blob/main/README.md).

You can find the documentation about our syntax, features, configuration in our book:
[askama.rs](https://askama.rs/).

[§](https://docs.rs#creating-askama-templates)Creating Askama templates

The main feature of Askama is the [ Template](https://docs.rs/trait.Template.html) derive macro
which reads your template code, so your

`struct` or `enum` can implement
the [trait and](https://docs.rs/trait.Template.html)

`Template`[, type-safe and fast:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html)

`Display````
#[derive(Template)]
#[template(
    ext = "html",
    source = "<p>© {{ year }} {{ enterprise|upper }}</p>"
)]
struct Footer<'a> {
    year: u16,
    enterprise: &'a str,
}
assert_eq!(
    Footer { year: 2025, enterprise: "<em>Askama</em> developers" }.to_string(),
    "<p>© 2025 <EM>ASKAMA</EM> DEVELOPERS</p>",
);
// In here you see can Askama's auto-escaping. You, the developer,
// can easily disable the auto-escaping with the `|safe` filter,
// but a malicious user cannot insert e.g. HTML scripts this way.
```
An Askama template is a `struct` or `enum` definition which provides the template
context combined with a UTF-8 encoded text file (or inline source).
Askama can be used to generate any kind of text-based format.
The template file’s extension may be used to provide content type hints.

A template consists of **text contents**, which are passed through as-is,
**expressions**, which get replaced with content while being rendered, and
**tags**, which control the template’s logic.
The template syntax is very similar to [Jinja](http://jinja.pocoo.org/),
as well as Jinja-derivatives like [Twig](https://twig.symfony.com/) or
[Tera](https://github.com/Keats/tera).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [filters](https://docs.rs/filters/index.html)
- Module for built-in filter functions

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- `dyn`-compatible- `Template`
- [Fast](https://docs.rs/trait.FastWritable.html)- Writable
- Types implementing this trait can be written without needing to employ an `fmt::Formatter`
- [Primitive](https://docs.rs/trait.PrimitiveType.html)- Type
- A type that is, references, or wraps a [primitive](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive/index.html)type

# axum - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/axum/^0.8.9/

## Expand description

axum is an HTTP routing and request-handling library that focuses on ergonomics and modularity.

[§](https://docs.rs#high-level-features)High-level features

- Route requests to handlers with a macro-free API.
- Declaratively parse requests using extractors.
- Simple and predictable error handling model.
- Generate responses with minimal boilerplate.
- Take full advantage of the `tower``tower-http`

In particular, the last point is what sets `axum` apart from other libraries / frameworks.
`axum` doesn’t have its own middleware system but instead uses
[ tower::Service](https://docs.rs/tower-service/0.3.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tower_service/trait.Service.html). This means

`axum` gets timeouts, tracing, compression,
authorization, and more, for free. It also enables you to share middleware with
applications written using [or](http://crates.io/crates/hyper)

`hyper`[.](http://crates.io/crates/tonic)

`tonic`[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

axum is designed to work with [tokio](https://docs.rs/tokio/1.47.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tokio/index.html) and [hyper](https://docs.rs/hyper/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/hyper/index.html). Runtime and
transport layer independence is not a goal, at least for the time being.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The “Hello, World!” of axum is:

```
use axum::{
    routing::get,
    Router,
};
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    // build our application with a single route
    let app = Router::new().route("/", get(|| async { "Hello, World!" }));
    // run our app with hyper, listening globally on port 3000
    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("0.0.0.0:3000").await.unwrap();
    axum::serve(listener, app).await.unwrap();
}
```
Note using `#[tokio::main]` requires you enable tokio’s `macros` and `rt-multi-thread` features
or just `full` to enable all features (`cargo add tokio --features macros,rt-multi-thread`).

[§](https://docs.rs#routing)Routing

[ Router](https://docs.rs/struct.Router.html) is used to set up which paths go to which services:

```
use axum::{Router, routing::get};
// our router
let app = Router::new()
    .route("/", get(root))
    .route("/foo", get(get_foo).post(post_foo))
    .route("/foo/bar", get(foo_bar));
// which calls one of these handlers
async fn root() {}
async fn get_foo() {}
async fn post_foo() {}
async fn foo_bar() {}
```
See [ Router](https://docs.rs/struct.Router.html) for more details on routing.

[§](https://docs.rs#handlers)Handlers

In axum a “handler” is an async function that accepts zero or more
[“extractors”](https://docs.rs/extract/index.html) as arguments and returns something that
can be converted [into a response](https://docs.rs/response/index.html).

Handlers are where your application logic lives and axum applications are built by routing between handlers.

See [ handler](https://docs.rs/handler/index.html) for more details on handlers.

[§](https://docs.rs#extractors)Extractors

An extractor is a type that implements [ FromRequest](https://docs.rs/extract/trait.FromRequest.html) or

[. Extractors are how you pick apart the incoming request to get the parts your handler needs.](https://docs.rs/extract/trait.FromRequestParts.html)

`FromRequestParts````
use axum::extract::{Path, Query, Json};
use std::collections::HashMap;
// `Path` gives you the path parameters and deserializes them.
async fn path(Path(user_id): Path<u32>) {}
// `Query` gives you the query parameters and deserializes them.
async fn query(Query(params): Query<HashMap<String, String>>) {}
// Buffer the request body and deserialize it as JSON into a
// `serde_json::Value`. `Json` supports any type that implements
// `serde::Deserialize`.
async fn json(Json(payload): Json<serde_json::Value>) {}
```
See [ extract](https://docs.rs/extract/index.html) for more details on extractors.

[§](https://docs.rs#responses)Responses

Anything that implements [ IntoResponse](https://docs.rs/response/trait.IntoResponse.html) can be returned from handlers.

```
use axum::{
    body::Body,
    routing::get,
    response::Json,
    Router,
};
use serde_json::{Value, json};
// `&'static str` becomes a `200 OK` with `content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8`
async fn plain_text() -> &'static str {
    "foo"
}
// `Json` gives a content-type of `application/json` and works with any type
// that implements `serde::Serialize`
async fn json() -> Json<Value> {
    Json(json!({ "data": 42 }))
}
let app = Router::new()
    .route("/plain_text", get(plain_text))
    .route("/json", get(json));
```
See [ response](https://docs.rs/response/index.html) for more details on building responses.

[§](https://docs.rs#error-handling)Error handling

axum aims to have a simple and predictable error handling model. That means it is simple to convert errors into responses and you are guaranteed that all errors are handled.

See [ error_handling](https://docs.rs/error_handling/index.html) for more details on axum’s
error handling model and how to handle errors gracefully.

[§](https://docs.rs#middleware)Middleware

There are several different ways to write middleware for axum. See
[ middleware](https://docs.rs/middleware/index.html) for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#sharing-state-with-handlers)Sharing state with handlers

It is common to share some state between handlers. For example, a pool of database connections or clients to other services may need to be shared.

The four most common ways of doing that are:

- Using the `State`
- Using request extensions
- Using closure captures
- Using task-local variables

```
use axum::{
    extract::State,
    routing::get,
    Router,
};
use std::sync::Arc;
struct AppState {
    // ...
}
let shared_state = Arc::new(AppState { /* ... */ });
let app = Router::new()
    .route("/", get(handler))
    .with_state(shared_state);
async fn handler(
    State(state): State<Arc<AppState>>,
) {
    // ...
}
```
State is cloned for every request. Wrapping your state in `Arc` makes those
clones cheap. If all fields are already cheap to clone (for example, each field
is itself an `Arc` or a copy type), you can `#[derive(Clone)]` directly on the
struct instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#substates-with-fromref)Substates with `FromRef`

When a handler only needs part of the application state, use [ FromRef](https://docs.rs/extract/trait.FromRef.html) to extract
a substate. Implement the trait manually, or derive it with

`#[derive(FromRef)]`
(requires the `macros` feature):```
use axum::{Router, routing::get, extract::{State, FromRef}};
#[derive(Clone)]
struct AppState {
    api_state: ApiState,
}
#[derive(Clone)]
struct ApiState {}
// Teach axum how to produce an `ApiState` from a reference to `AppState`.
impl FromRef<AppState> for ApiState {
    fn from_ref(app_state: &AppState) -> ApiState {
        app_state.api_state.clone()
    }
}
let app = Router::new()
    .route("/", get(handler))
    .with_state(AppState { api_state: ApiState {} });
// This handler receives only the `ApiState` slice; it never sees `AppState`.
async fn handler(State(api_state): State<ApiState>) {}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-routers-type-parameter)The `Router<S>` type parameter

`Router<S>` when `S` is not `()` means a router that is *missing* a state of type `S`. Calling
[ .with_state(s)](https://docs.rs/struct.Router.html#method.with_state) provides that state and typically produces a

`Router<()>`, which is the only form that can be passed to [. See](https://docs.rs/fn.serve.html)

`serve()`[for a full explanation.](https://docs.rs/struct.Router.html#method.with_state)

`Router::with_state`You should prefer using [ State](https://docs.rs/extract/struct.State.html) if possible since it’s more type safe. The downside is that
it’s less dynamic than task-local variables and request extensions.

See [ State](https://docs.rs/extract/struct.State.html) for more details about accessing state.

[§](https://docs.rs#using-request-extensions)Using request extensions

Another way to share state with handlers is using [ Extension](https://docs.rs/struct.Extension.html) as
layer and extractor:

```
use axum::{
    extract::Extension,
    routing::get,
    Router,
};
use std::sync::Arc;
struct AppState {
    // ...
}
let shared_state = Arc::new(AppState { /* ... */ });
let app = Router::new()
    .route("/", get(handler))
    .layer(Extension(shared_state));
async fn handler(
    Extension(state): Extension<Arc<AppState>>,
) {
    // ...
}
```
The downside to this approach is that you’ll get runtime errors
(specifically a `500 Internal Server Error` response) if you try and extract
an extension that doesn’t exist, perhaps because you forgot to add the
middleware or because you’re extracting the wrong type.

[§](https://docs.rs#using-closure-captures)Using closure captures

State can also be passed directly to handlers using closure captures:

```
use axum::{
    Json,
    extract::{Extension, Path},
    routing::{get, post},
    Router,
};
use std::sync::Arc;
use serde::Deserialize;
struct AppState {
    // ...
}
let shared_state = Arc::new(AppState { /* ... */ });
let app = Router::new()
    .route(
        "/users",
        post({
            let shared_state = Arc::clone(&shared_state);
            move |body| create_user(body, shared_state)
        }),
    )
    .route(
        "/users/{id}",
        get({
            let shared_state = Arc::clone(&shared_state);
            move |path| get_user(path, shared_state)
        }),
    );
async fn get_user(Path(user_id): Path<String>, state: Arc<AppState>) {
    // ...
}
async fn create_user(Json(payload): Json<CreateUserPayload>, state: Arc<AppState>) {
    // ...
}
#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct CreateUserPayload {
    // ...
}
```
The downside to this approach is that it’s the most verbose approach.

[§](https://docs.rs#using-task-local-variables)Using task-local variables

This also allows to share state with `IntoResponse` implementations:

```
use axum::{
    extract::Request,
    http::{header, StatusCode},
    middleware::{self, Next},
    response::{IntoResponse, Response},
    routing::get,
    Router,
};
use tokio::task_local;
#[derive(Clone)]
struct CurrentUser {
    name: String,
}
task_local! {
    pub static USER: CurrentUser;
}
async fn auth(req: Request, next: Next) -> Result<Response, StatusCode> {
    let auth_header = req
        .headers()
        .get(header::AUTHORIZATION)
        .and_then(|header| header.to_str().ok())
        .ok_or(StatusCode::UNAUTHORIZED)?;
    if let Some(current_user) = authorize_current_user(auth_header).await {
        // State is setup here in the middleware
        Ok(USER.scope(current_user, next.run(req)).await)
    } else {
        Err(StatusCode::UNAUTHORIZED)
    }
}
async fn authorize_current_user(auth_token: &str) -> Option<CurrentUser> {
    Some(CurrentUser {
        name: auth_token.to_string(),
    })
}
struct UserResponse;
impl IntoResponse for UserResponse {
    fn into_response(self) -> Response {
        // State is accessed here in the IntoResponse implementation
        let current_user = USER.with(|u| u.clone());
        (StatusCode::OK, current_user.name).into_response()
    }
}
async fn handler() -> UserResponse {
    UserResponse
}
let app: Router = Router::new()
    .route("/", get(handler))
    .route_layer(middleware::from_fn(auth));
```
The main downside to this approach is that it only works when the async executor being used
has the concept of task-local variables. The example above uses
[tokio’s  task_local macro](https://docs.rs/tokio/1/tokio/macro.task_local.html).
smol does not yet offer equivalent functionality at the time of writing (see

[this GitHub issue](https://github.com/smol-rs/async-executor/issues/139)).

[§](https://docs.rs#building-integrations-for-axum)Building integrations for axum

Libraries authors that want to provide [ FromRequest](https://docs.rs/extract/trait.FromRequest.html),

[, or](https://docs.rs/extract/trait.FromRequestParts.html)

`FromRequestParts`[implementations should depend on the](https://docs.rs/response/trait.IntoResponse.html)

`IntoResponse`[crate, instead of](http://crates.io/crates/axum-core)

`axum-core``axum` if
possible. [contains core types and traits and is less likely to receive breaking changes.](http://crates.io/crates/axum-core)

`axum-core`[§](https://docs.rs#required-dependencies)Required dependencies

To use axum there are a few dependencies you have to pull in as well:

```
[dependencies]
axum = "<latest-version>"
tokio = { version = "<latest-version>", features = ["full"] }
tower = "<latest-version>"
```
The `"full"` feature for tokio isn’t necessary but it’s the easiest way to get started.

Tower isn’t strictly necessary either but helpful for testing. See the testing example in the repo to learn more about testing axum apps.

# datafusion - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/datafusion/^53.1.0/

## Expand description

[DataFusion](https://datafusion.apache.org/) is an extensible query engine written in Rust that
uses [Apache Arrow](https://arrow.apache.org) as its in-memory format. DataFusion’s target users are
developers building fast and feature rich database and analytic systems,
customized to particular workloads. Please see the [DataFusion website](https://datafusion.apache.org) for
additional documentation, [use cases](https://datafusion.apache.org/user-guide/introduction.html#use-cases) and examples.

“Out of the box,” DataFusion offers [SQL](https://datafusion.apache.org/user-guide/sql/index.html) and [ Dataframe](https://docs.rs/dataframe/struct.DataFrame.html) APIs,
excellent

[performance](https://benchmark.clickhouse.com/), built-in support for CSV, Parquet, JSON, and Avro, extensive customization, and a great community.

[Python Bindings](https://github.com/apache/datafusion-python)are also available.

DataFusion features a full query planner, a columnar, streaming, multi-threaded,
vectorized execution engine, and partitioned data  sources. You can
customize DataFusion at almost all points including additional data sources,
query languages, functions, custom operators and more.
See the [Architecture](https://docs.rs#architecture) section below for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

The main entry point for interacting with DataFusion is the
[ SessionContext](https://docs.rs/execution/context/struct.SessionContext.html).

[s represent expressions such as](https://docs.rs/prelude/enum.Expr.html)

`Expr``a + b`.[§](https://docs.rs#dataframe)DataFrame

To execute a query against data stored
in a CSV file using a [ DataFrame](https://docs.rs/dataframe/struct.DataFrame.html):

```
let ctx = SessionContext::new();
// create the dataframe
let df = ctx
    .read_csv("tests/data/example.csv", CsvReadOptions::new())
    .await?;
// create a plan
let df = df
    .filter(col("a").lt_eq(col("b")))?
    .aggregate(vec![col("a")], vec![min(col("b"))])?
    .limit(0, Some(100))?;
// execute the plan
let results: Vec<RecordBatch> = df.collect().await?;
// format the results
let pretty_results =
    arrow::util::pretty::pretty_format_batches(&results)?.to_string();
let expected = vec![
    "+---+----------------+",
    "| a | min(?table?.b) |",
    "+---+----------------+",
    "| 1 | 2              |",
    "+---+----------------+",
];
assert_eq!(pretty_results.trim().lines().collect::<Vec<_>>(), expected);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#sql)SQL

To execute a query against a CSV file using [SQL](https://datafusion.apache.org/user-guide/sql/index.html):

```
let ctx = SessionContext::new();
ctx.register_csv("example", "tests/data/example.csv", CsvReadOptions::new())
    .await?;
// create a plan
let df = ctx
    .sql("SELECT a, MIN(b) FROM example WHERE a <= b GROUP BY a LIMIT 100")
    .await?;
// execute the plan
let results: Vec<RecordBatch> = df.collect().await?;
// format the results
let pretty_results =
    arrow::util::pretty::pretty_format_batches(&results)?.to_string();
let expected = vec![
    "+---+----------------+",
    "| a | min(example.b) |",
    "+---+----------------+",
    "| 1 | 2              |",
    "+---+----------------+",
];
assert_eq!(pretty_results.trim().lines().collect::<Vec<_>>(), expected);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#more-examples)More Examples

There are many additional annotated examples of using DataFusion in the [datafusion-examples](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/tree/main/datafusion-examples) directory.

[§](https://docs.rs#architecture)Architecture

You can find a formal description of DataFusion’s architecture in our
[SIGMOD 2024 Paper](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3626246.3653368).

[§](https://docs.rs#design-goals)Design Goals

DataFusion’s Architecture Goals are:

-
Work “out of the box”: Provide a very fast, world class query engine with minimal setup or required configuration.
-
Customizable everything: All behavior should be customizable by implementing traits.
-
Architecturally boring 🥱: Follow industrial best practice rather than trying cutting edge, but unproven, techniques.

With these principles, users start with a basic, high-performance engine and specialize it over time to suit their needs and available engineering capacity.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview--presentations)Overview  Presentations

The following presentations offer high level overviews of the different components and how they interact together.

- [Apr 2023]: The Apache DataFusion Architecture talks
- [July 2022]: DataFusion and Arrow: Supercharge Your Data Analytical Tool with a Rusty Query Engine: [recording](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Rii1VTn3seQ)and[slides](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1q1bPibvu64k2b7LPi7Yyb0k3gA1BiUYiUbEklqW1Ckc/view#slide=id.g11054eeab4c_0_1165)
- [March 2021]: The DataFusion architecture is described in *Query Engine Design and the Rust-Based DataFusion in Apache Arrow*:[recording](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K6eCAVEk4kU)(DataFusion content starts[~ 15 minutes in](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K6eCAVEk4kU&t=875s)) and[slides](https://www.slideshare.net/influxdata/influxdb-iox-tech-talks-query-engine-design-and-the-rustbased-datafusion-in-apache-arrow-244161934)
- [February 2021]: How DataFusion is used within the Ballista Project is described in *Ballista: Distributed Compute with Rust and Apache Arrow*:[recording](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZZHQaOap9pQ)

[§](https://docs.rs#customization-and-extension)Customization and Extension

DataFusion is designed to be highly extensible, so you can
start with a working, full featured engine, and then
specialize any behavior for your use case. For example,
some projects may add custom [ ExecutionPlan](https://docs.rs/physical_plan/trait.ExecutionPlan.html) operators, or create their own
query language that directly creates

[rather than using the built in SQL planner,](https://docs.rs/logical_expr/enum.LogicalPlan.html)

`LogicalPlan`[.](https://docs.rs/sql/planner/struct.SqlToRel.html)

`SqlToRel`In order to achieve this, DataFusion supports extension at many points:

- read from any datasource (`TableProvider`
- define your own catalogs, schemas, and table lists (`catalog``CatalogProvider`
- build your own query language or plans (`LogicalPlanBuilder`
- declare and use user-defined functions (`ScalarUDF``AggregateUDF``WindowUDF`
- add custom plan rewrite passes (`AnalyzerRule``OptimizerRule``PhysicalOptimizerRule`
- extend the planner to use user-defined logical and physical nodes (`QueryPlanner`

You can find examples of each of them in the [datafusion-examples](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/tree/main/datafusion-examples) directory.

[§](https://docs.rs#query-planning-and-execution-overview)Query Planning and Execution Overview

[§](https://docs.rs#sql-1)SQL

```
                Parsed with            SqlToRel creates
                sqlparser              initial plan
┌───────────────┐           ┌─────────┐             ┌─────────────┐
│   SELECT *    │           │Query {  │             │Project      │
│   FROM ...    │──────────▶│..       │────────────▶│  TableScan  │
│               │           │}        │             │    ...      │
└───────────────┘           └─────────┘             └─────────────┘
  SQL String                 sqlparser               LogicalPlan
                             AST nodes
```
-
The query string is parsed to an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) `Statement`[sqlparser](https://docs.rs/sqlparser/latest/sqlparser).
-
The AST is converted to a `LogicalPlan``Expr``SqlToRel`

[§](https://docs.rs#dataframe-1)DataFrame

When executing plans using the [ DataFrame](https://docs.rs/dataframe/struct.DataFrame.html) API, the process is
identical as with SQL, except the DataFrame API builds the

[directly using](https://docs.rs/logical_expr/enum.LogicalPlan.html)

`LogicalPlan`[. Systems that have their own custom query languages typically also build](https://docs.rs/logical_expr/struct.LogicalPlanBuilder.html)

`LogicalPlanBuilder`[directly.](https://docs.rs/logical_expr/enum.LogicalPlan.html)

`LogicalPlan`[§](https://docs.rs#planning)Planning

```
            AnalyzerRules and      PhysicalPlanner          PhysicalOptimizerRules
            OptimizerRules         creates ExecutionPlan    improve performance
            rewrite plan
┌─────────────┐        ┌─────────────┐      ┌─────────────────┐        ┌─────────────────┐
│Project      │        │Project(x, y)│      │ProjectExec      │        │ProjectExec      │
│  TableScan  │──...──▶│  TableScan  │─────▶│  ...            │──...──▶│  ...            │
│    ...      │        │    ...      │      │   DataSourceExec│        │   DataSourceExec│
└─────────────┘        └─────────────┘      └─────────────────┘        └─────────────────┘
 LogicalPlan            LogicalPlan         ExecutionPlan             ExecutionPlan
```
To process large datasets with many rows as efficiently as possible, significant effort is spent planning and optimizing, in the following manner:

-
The `LogicalPlan``AnalyzerRule`
-
The `LogicalPlan``OptimizerRule`
-
The `LogicalPlan``ExecutionPlan``PhysicalPlanner`
-
The `ExecutionPlan``PhysicalOptimizerRule`

[§](https://docs.rs#plan-representations)Plan Representations

[§](https://docs.rs#logical-plans)Logical Plans

Logical planning yields [ LogicalPlan](https://docs.rs/logical_expr/enum.LogicalPlan.html) nodes and

[representing expressions which are](https://docs.rs/prelude/enum.Expr.html)

`Expr`[aware and represent statements independent of how they are physically executed. A](https://docs.rs/common/arrow/datatypes/struct.Schema.html)

`Schema`[is a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of other](https://docs.rs/logical_expr/enum.LogicalPlan.html)

`LogicalPlan`[s, each potentially containing embedded](https://docs.rs/logical_expr/enum.LogicalPlan.html)

`LogicalPlan`[s.](https://docs.rs/prelude/enum.Expr.html)

`Expr`[ LogicalPlan](https://docs.rs/logical_expr/enum.LogicalPlan.html)s can be rewritten with

[API, see the](https://docs.rs/common/tree_node/trait.TreeNode.html)

`TreeNode`[for more details.](https://docs.rs/logical_expr/logical_plan/tree_node/index.html)

`tree_node module`[ Expr](https://docs.rs/prelude/enum.Expr.html)s can also be rewritten with

[API and simplified using](https://docs.rs/common/tree_node/trait.TreeNode.html)

`TreeNode`[. Examples of working with and executing](https://docs.rs/optimizer/simplify_expressions/struct.ExprSimplifier.html)

`ExprSimplifier`[s can be found in the](https://docs.rs/prelude/enum.Expr.html)

`Expr`[example](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/main/datafusion-examples/examples/query_planning/expr_api.rs)

`expr_api`.rs[§](https://docs.rs#physical-plans)Physical Plans

An [ ExecutionPlan](https://docs.rs/physical_plan/trait.ExecutionPlan.html) (sometimes referred to as a “physical plan”)
is a plan that can be executed against data. It a DAG of other

[s each potentially containing expressions that implement the](https://docs.rs/physical_plan/trait.ExecutionPlan.html)

`ExecutionPlan`[trait.](https://docs.rs/physical_expr/trait.PhysicalExpr.html)

`PhysicalExpr`Compared to a [ LogicalPlan](https://docs.rs/logical_expr/enum.LogicalPlan.html), an

[has additional concrete information about how to perform calculations (e.g. hash vs merge join), and how data flows during execution (e.g. partitioning and sortedness).](https://docs.rs/physical_plan/trait.ExecutionPlan.html)

`ExecutionPlan`[cp_solver](https://docs.rs/physical_expr/intervals/cp_solver/index.html) performs range propagation analysis on [ PhysicalExpr](https://docs.rs/physical_expr/trait.PhysicalExpr.html)s and

[can prove certain boolean](https://docs.rs/physical_optimizer/pruning/struct.PruningPredicate.html)

`PruningPredicate`[s used for filtering can never be](https://docs.rs/physical_expr/trait.PhysicalExpr.html)

`PhysicalExpr``true` using additional statistical information.[§](https://docs.rs#execution)Execution

```
           ExecutionPlan::execute             Calling next() on the
           produces a stream                  stream produces the data
┌────────────────┐      ┌─────────────────────────┐         ┌────────────┐
│ProjectExec     │      │impl                     │    ┌───▶│RecordBatch │
│  ...           │─────▶│SendableRecordBatchStream│────┤    └────────────┘

              │                                        │

```
[ ExecutionPlan](https://docs.rs/physical_plan/trait.ExecutionPlan.html)s process data using the

[Apache Arrow](https://arrow.apache.org)memory format, making heavy use of functions from the

[arrow](https://docs.rs/common/arrow/index.html)crate. Values are represented with

[, which are either](https://docs.rs/logical_expr/enum.ColumnarValue.html)

`ColumnarValue`[(single constant values) or](https://docs.rs/scalar/enum.ScalarValue.html)

`ScalarValue`[(Arrow Arrays).](https://docs.rs/common/arrow/array/type.ArrayRef.html)

`ArrayRef`Calling [ execute](https://docs.rs/physical_plan/trait.ExecutionPlan.html#tymethod.execute) produces 1 or more partitions of data,
as a

[, which implements a pull based execution API. Calling](https://docs.rs/execution/type.SendableRecordBatchStream.html)

`SendableRecordBatchStream`

`next()``.await` will incrementally compute and return the next
[. Balanced parallelism is achieved using](https://docs.rs/common/arrow/array/struct.RecordBatch.html)

`RecordBatch`[Volcano style](https://doi.org/10.1145/93605.98720)“Exchange” operations implemented by

[.](https://docs.rs/datafusion/latest/datafusion/physical_plan/repartition/struct.RepartitionExec.html)

`RepartitionExec`While some recent research such as [Morsel-Driven Parallelism](https://db.in.tum.de/~leis/papers/morsels.pdf) describes challenges
with the pull style Volcano execution model on NUMA architectures, in practice DataFusion achieves
similar scalability as systems that use push driven schedulers [such as DuckDB](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/issues/1583).
See the [DataFusion paper in SIGMOD 2024](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/files/15149988/DataFusion_Query_Engine___SIGMOD_2024-FINAL-mk4.pdf) for more details.

See the [implementors of  ExecutionPlan](https://docs.rs/datafusion/latest/datafusion/physical_plan/trait.ExecutionPlan.html#implementors) for a list of physical operators available.

[§](https://docs.rs#streaming-execution)Streaming Execution

DataFusion is a “streaming” query engine which means [ ExecutionPlan](https://docs.rs/physical_plan/trait.ExecutionPlan.html)s incrementally
read from their input(s) and compute output one

[at a time by continually polling](https://docs.rs/common/arrow/array/struct.RecordBatch.html)

`RecordBatch`[s. Output and intermediate](https://docs.rs/execution/type.SendableRecordBatchStream.html)

`SendableRecordBatchStream`[s each have approximately](https://docs.rs/common/arrow/array/struct.RecordBatch.html)

`RecordBatch``batch_size` rows,
which amortizes per-batch overhead of execution.Note that certain operations, sometimes called “pipeline breakers”,
(for example full sorts or hash aggregations) are fundamentally non streaming and
must read their input fully before producing **any** output. As much as possible,
other operators read a single [ RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/common/arrow/array/struct.RecordBatch.html) from their input to produce a
single

[as output.](https://docs.rs/common/arrow/array/struct.RecordBatch.html)

`RecordBatch`For example, given this SQL:

`SELECT name FROM 'data.parquet' WHERE id > 10`An simplified DataFusion execution plan is shown below. It first reads
data from the Parquet file, then applies the filter, then the projection,
and finally produces output. Each step processes one [ RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/common/arrow/array/struct.RecordBatch.html) at a
time. Multiple batches are processed concurrently on different CPU cores
for plans with multiple partitions.

```
┌─────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────┐    ┌──────────┐
│ Parquet     │───▶│ DataSource   │───▶│ FilterExec     │───▶│ ProjectionExec   │───▶│ Results  │
│ File        │    │              │    │                │    │                  │    │          │
└─────────────┘    └──────────────┘    └────────────────┘    └──────────────────┘    └──────────┘
                   (reads data)        (id > 10)             (keeps "name" col)
                   RecordBatch ───▶    RecordBatch ────▶     RecordBatch ────▶        RecordBatch
```
DataFusion uses the classic “pull” based control flow (explained more in the next section) to implement streaming execution. As an example, consider the following SQL query:

`SELECT date_trunc('month', time) FROM data WHERE id IN (10,20,30);`The diagram below shows the call sequence when a consumer calls [ next()](https://docs.rs/futures-util/0.3.32/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/futures_util/stream/stream/trait.StreamExt.html#method.next) to
get the next

[of output. While it is possible that some steps run on different threads, typically tokio will use the same thread that called](https://docs.rs/common/arrow/array/struct.RecordBatch.html)

`RecordBatch`[to read from the input, apply the filter, and return the results without interleaving any other operations. This results in excellent cache locality as the same CPU core that produces the data often consumes it immediately as well.](https://docs.rs/futures-util/0.3.32/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/futures_util/stream/stream/trait.StreamExt.html#method.next)

`next()````
Step 3: FilterExec calls next()       Step 2: ProjectionExec calls
        on input Stream                  next() on input Stream
        ┌ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─      ┌ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ┐
                           │                                               Step 1: Consumer
        ▼                        ▼                           │               calls next()
┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓     ┏━━━━━┻━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓      ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
┃                ┃     ┃                   ┃      ┃                        ◀ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─

┃                ┃     ┃                   ┃      ┃                        ┣ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ▶
┃                ┃     ┃                   ┃      ┃                        ┃
┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛     ┗━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━┛      ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛
        │                  ▲                                 ▲          Step 6: ProjectionExec
                           │     │                           │        computes date_trunc into a
        └ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─       ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─          new RecordBatch returned
             ┌─────────────────────┐                ┌─────────────┐          from client
             │     RecordBatch     │                │ RecordBatch │
             └─────────────────────┘                └─────────────┘
          Step 4: DataSource returns a        Step 5: FilterExec returns a new
               single RecordBatch            RecordBatch with only matching rows
