# tower - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tower/^0.5.3/

## Expand description

`async fn(Request) -> Result<Response, Error>`

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

Tower is a library of modular and reusable components for building robust networking clients and servers.

Tower provides a simple core abstraction, the [ Service](https://docs.rs/trait.Service.html) trait, which
represents an asynchronous function taking a request and returning either a
response or an error. This abstraction can be used to model both clients and
servers.

Generic components, like [ timeout](https://docs.rs/timeout/index.html),

[rate limiting](https://docs.rs/limit/rate/index.html), and

[load balancing](https://docs.rs/balance/index.html), can be modeled as

[s that wrap some inner service and apply additional behavior before or after the inner service is called. This allows implementing these components in a protocol-agnostic, composable way. Typically, such services are referred to as](https://docs.rs/trait.Service.html)

`Service`*middleware*.

An additional abstraction, the [ Layer](https://docs.rs/trait.Layer.html) trait, is used to compose
middleware with

[s. If a](https://docs.rs/trait.Service.html)

`Service`[can be thought of as an asynchronous function from a request type to a response type, a](https://docs.rs/trait.Service.html)

`Service`[is a function taking a](https://docs.rs/trait.Layer.html)

`Layer`[of one type and returning a](https://docs.rs/trait.Service.html)

`Service`[of a different type. The](https://docs.rs/trait.Service.html)

`Service`[type is used to add middleware to a service by composing it with multiple](https://docs.rs/struct.ServiceBuilder.html)

`ServiceBuilder`[s.](https://docs.rs/trait.Layer.html)

`Layer`[§](https://docs.rs#the-tower-ecosystem)The Tower Ecosystem

Tower is made up of the following crates:

- `tower`
- `tower-service`
- `tower-layer`
- `tower-test`

Since the [ Service](https://docs.rs/trait.Service.html) and

[traits are important integration points for all libraries using Tower, they are kept as stable as possible, and breaking changes are made rarely. Therefore, they are defined in separate crates,](https://docs.rs/trait.Layer.html)

`Layer`[and](https://crates.io/crates/tower-service)

`tower-service`[. This crate contains re-exports of those core traits, implementations of commonly-used middleware, and](https://crates.io/crates/tower-layer)

`tower-layer`[utilities](https://docs.rs/trait.ServiceExt.html)for working with

[s and](https://docs.rs/trait.Service.html)

`Service`[s. Finally, the](https://docs.rs/trait.Layer.html)

`Layer`[crate provides tools for testing programs using Tower.](https://crates.io/crates/tower-test)

`tower-test`[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Tower provides an abstraction layer, and generic implementations of various
middleware. This means that the `tower` crate on its own does *not* provide
a working implementation of a network client or server. Instead, Tower’s
[ Service trait](https://docs.rs/trait.Service.html) provides an integration point between
application code, libraries providing middleware implementations, and
libraries that implement servers and/or clients for various network
protocols.

Depending on your particular use case, you might use Tower in several ways:

-
**Implementing application logic**for a networked program. You might use the`Service`[provided by this crate](https://docs.rs#modules)and by other libraries to add functionality to clients and servers provided by one or more protocol implementations.
-
**Implementing middleware**to add custom behavior to network clients and servers in a reusable manner. This might be general-purpose middleware (and if it is, please consider releasing your middleware as a library for other Tower users!) or application-specific behavior that needs to be shared between multiple clients or servers.
-
**Implementing a network protocol**. Libraries that implement network protocols (such as HTTP) can depend on`tower-service`to use the`Service``Service``Service`Additionally, when a network protocol requires functionality already provided by existing Tower middleware, a protocol implementation might use Tower middleware internally, as well as as an integration point.

[§](https://docs.rs#library-support)Library Support

A number of third-party libraries support Tower and the [ Service](https://docs.rs/trait.Service.html) trait.
The following is an incomplete list of such libraries:

- `hyper`
- `tonic`- [gRPC-over-HTTP/2](https://grpc.io)implementation built on top of- `hyper`- [here](https://github.com/hyperium/tonic/tree/master/examples/src/tower)for examples of using- `tonic`
- `warp`- [here](https://docs.rs/warp/0.2.5/warp/fn.service.html)for details on using- `warp`
- `tower-lsp`- [Language Server Protocol](https://microsoft.github.io/language-server-protocol/)based on Tower.

If you’re the maintainer of a crate that supports Tower, we’d love to add
your crate to this list! Please [open a PR](https://github.com/tower-rs/tower/compare) adding a brief description of
your library!

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting Started

If you’re brand new to Tower and want to start with the basics, we recommend you
check out some of our [guides](https://github.com/tower-rs/tower/tree/master/guides).

The various middleware implementations provided by this crate are feature flagged, so that users can only compile the parts of Tower they need. By default, all the optional middleware are disabled.

To get started using all of Tower’s optional middleware, add this to your
`Cargo.toml`:

`tower = { version = "0.4", features = ["full"] }`Alternatively, you can only enable some features. For example, to enable
only the [ retry](https://docs.rs/retry/index.html) and

[middleware, write:](https://docs.rs/timeout/index.html)

`timeout``tower = { version = "0.4", features = ["retry", "timeout"] }`See [here](https://docs.rs#modules) for a complete list of all middleware provided by
Tower.

[§](https://docs.rs#supported-rust-versions)Supported Rust Versions

Tower will keep a rolling MSRV (minimum supported Rust version) policy of **at
least** 6 months. When increasing the MSRV, the new Rust version must have been
released at least six months ago. The current MSRV is 1.64.0.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [balance](https://docs.rs/balance/index.html)- `balance`
- Middleware that allows balancing load among multiple services.
- [buffer](https://docs.rs/buffer/index.html)- `buffer`
- Middleware that provides a buffered mpsc channel to a service.
- [builder](https://docs.rs/builder/index.html)
- Builder types to compose layers and services

- Trait aliases for Services that produce specific types of Responses.
- [ready_](https://docs.rs/ready_cache/index.html)- cache - `ready-cache`
- A cache of services
- [reconnect](https://docs.rs/reconnect/index.html)- `reconnect`
- Reconnect services when they fail.
- [retry](https://docs.rs/retry/index.html)- `retry`
- Middleware for retrying “failed” requests.
- [spawn_](https://docs.rs/spawn_ready/index.html)- ready - `spawn-ready`
- When an underlying service is not ready, drive it to readiness on a background task.
- [steer](https://docs.rs/steer/index.html)- `steer`
- This module provides functionality to aid managing routing requests between `Service`
- [timeout](https://docs.rs/timeout/index.html)- `timeout`
- Middleware that applies a timeout to requests.
- [util](https://docs.rs/util/index.html)- `util`
- Various utility types and functions that are generally used with Tower.

# krishiv_ui - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/krishiv-ui/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/target-redirect/krishiv_ui/

## Expand description

R2 status API and server-rendered Web UI.

This crate exposes scheduler snapshots as a small Rust-native operations surface. It intentionally depends on the in-process R2 scheduler model rather than introducing Kubernetes clients or a separate frontend build.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [UiState](https://docs.rs/struct.UiState.html)
- Shared state for the R2 status server.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [UiError](https://docs.rs/enum.UiError.html)
- UI construction and handler errors.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [demo_](https://docs.rs/fn.demo_state.html)- state
- Create a deterministic demo state for local UI development and tests.
- [embedded_](https://docs.rs/fn.embedded_router.html)- router
- Build the UI-specific routes (jobs, executors, SQL editor, health dashboard) for embedding inside the coordinator HTTP server.
- [empty_](https://docs.rs/fn.empty_state.html)- state
- Create an empty active coordinator state for real status serving.
- [router](https://docs.rs/fn.router.html)
- Build the R2 UI router.
- [router_](https://docs.rs/fn.router_with_token.html)- with_ - token
- Build the R2 UI router with an explicit auth token. When `Some`, the same routes as`router()`get wrapped in the bearer-token middleware. When`None`, the router behaves identically to a`KRISHIV_UI_TOKEN`-unset build.
- [serve](https://docs.rs/fn.serve.html)
- Serve the R2 status API and Web UI with an existing listener.

Task execution engine for running dataflow stages on worker nodes.

- Runs dataflow operators (filter, project, aggregate, join)

# base64 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/base64/^0.22.1/

## Expand description

Correct, fast, and configurable [base64](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Base64) decoding and encoding. Base64
transports binary data efficiently in contexts where only plain text is
allowed.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Use an [ Engine](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html) to decode or encode base64, configured with the base64
alphabet and padding behavior best suited to your application.

[§](https://docs.rs#engine-setup)Engine setup

There is more than one way to encode a stream of bytes as “base64”.
Different applications use different encoding
[alphabets](https://docs.rs/alphabet/struct.Alphabet.html) and
[padding behaviors](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurposeConfig.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#encoding-alphabet)Encoding alphabet

Almost all base64 [alphabets](https://docs.rs/alphabet/struct.Alphabet.html) use `A-Z`, `a-z`, and
`0-9`, which gives nearly 64 characters (26 + 26 + 10 = 62), but they differ
in their choice of their final 2.

Most applications use the [standard](https://docs.rs/alphabet/constant.STANDARD.html) alphabet specified
in [RFC 4648](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4648#section-4).  If that’s all you need, you can get started
quickly by using the pre-configured
[ STANDARD](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/constant.STANDARD.html) engine, which is also available
in the

[module as shown here, if you prefer a minimal](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)

`prelude``use`
footprint.```
use base64::prelude::*;
assert_eq!(BASE64_STANDARD.decode(b"+uwgVQA=")?, b"\xFA\xEC\x20\x55\0");
assert_eq!(BASE64_STANDARD.encode(b"\xFF\xEC\x20\x55\0"), "/+wgVQA=");
```
Other common alphabets are available in the [ alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/index.html) module.

[§](https://docs.rs#url-safe-alphabet)URL-safe alphabet

The standard alphabet uses `+` and `/` as its two non-alphanumeric tokens,
which cannot be safely used in URL’s without encoding them as `%2B` and
`%2F`.

To avoid that, some applications use a [“URL-safe” alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/constant.URL_SAFE.html),
which uses `-` and `_` instead. To use that alternative alphabet, use the
[ URL_SAFE](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/constant.URL_SAFE.html) engine. This example doesn’t
use

[to show what a more explicit](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)

`prelude``use` would look like.```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::URL_SAFE, Engine as _};
assert_eq!(URL_SAFE.decode(b"-uwgVQA=")?, b"\xFA\xEC\x20\x55\0");
assert_eq!(URL_SAFE.encode(b"\xFF\xEC\x20\x55\0"), "_-wgVQA=");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#padding-characters)Padding characters

Each base64 character represents 6 bits (2⁶ = 64) of the original binary data, and every 3 bytes of input binary data will encode to 4 base64 characters (8 bits × 3 = 6 bits × 4 = 24 bits).

When the input is not an even multiple of 3 bytes in length, [canonical](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4648#section-3.5)
base64 encoders insert padding characters at the end, so that the output
length is always a multiple of 4:

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, Engine as _};
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b""),    "");
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b"f"),   "Zg==");
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b"fo"),  "Zm8=");
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b"foo"), "Zm9v");
```
Canonical encoding ensures that base64 encodings will be exactly the same,
byte-for-byte, regardless of input length. But the `=` padding characters
aren’t necessary for decoding, and they may be omitted by using a
[ NO_PAD](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/constant.NO_PAD.html) configuration:

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD_NO_PAD, Engine as _};
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b""),    "");
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b"f"),   "Zg");
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b"fo"),  "Zm8");
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b"foo"), "Zm9v");
```
The pre-configured `NO_PAD` engines will reject inputs containing padding
`=` characters. To encode without padding and still accept padding while
decoding, create an [engine](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurpose.html) with
that [padding mode](https://docs.rs/engine/enum.DecodePaddingMode.html).

`assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.decode(b"Zm8="), Err(base64::DecodeError::InvalidPadding));`[§](https://docs.rs#further-customization)Further customization

Decoding and encoding behavior can be customized by creating an
[engine](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurpose.html) with an [alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/struct.Alphabet.html) and
[padding configuration](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurposeConfig.html):

```
use base64::{engine, alphabet, Engine as _};
// bizarro-world base64: +/ as the first symbols instead of the last
let alphabet =
    alphabet::Alphabet::new("+/ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789")
    .unwrap();
// a very weird config that encodes with padding but requires no padding when decoding...?
let crazy_config = engine::GeneralPurposeConfig::new()
    .with_decode_allow_trailing_bits(true)
    .with_encode_padding(true)
    .with_decode_padding_mode(engine::DecodePaddingMode::RequireNone);
let crazy_engine = engine::GeneralPurpose::new(&alphabet, crazy_config);
let encoded = crazy_engine.encode(b"abc 123");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#memory-allocation)Memory allocation

The [decode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.decode) and [encode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.encode) engine methods
allocate memory for their results – `decode` returns a `Vec<u8>` and
`encode` returns a `String`. To instead decode or encode into a buffer that
you allocated, use one of the alternative methods:

[§](https://docs.rs#decoding)Decoding

| Method | Output | Allocates memory |
|---|---|---|
| `Engine::decode` | returns a new `Vec<u8>` | always |
| `Engine::decode_vec` | appends to provided `Vec<u8>` | if `Vec`lacks capacity |
| `Engine::decode_slice` | writes to provided `&[u8]` | never |

[§](https://docs.rs#encoding)Encoding

| Method | Output | Allocates memory |
|---|---|---|
| `Engine::encode` | returns a new `String` | always |
| `Engine::encode_string` | appends to provided `String` | if `String`lacks capacity |
| `Engine::encode_slice` | writes to provided `&[u8]` | never |

[§](https://docs.rs#input-and-output)Input and output

The `base64` crate can [decode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.decode) and
[encode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.encode) values in memory, or
[ DecoderReader](https://docs.rs/read/struct.DecoderReader.html) and

[provide streaming decoding and encoding for any](https://docs.rs/write/struct.EncoderWriter.html)

`EncoderWriter`[readable](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Read.html)or

[writable](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html)byte stream.

[§](https://docs.rs#decoding-1)Decoding

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, read::DecoderReader};
let mut input = io::stdin();
let mut decoder = DecoderReader::new(&mut input, &STANDARD);
io::copy(&mut decoder, &mut io::stdout())?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#encoding-1)Encoding

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, write::EncoderWriter};
let mut output = io::stdout();
let mut encoder = EncoderWriter::new(&mut output, &STANDARD);
io::copy(&mut io::stdin(), &mut encoder)?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#display)Display

If you only need a base64 representation for implementing the
[ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html) trait, use

[:](https://docs.rs/display/struct.Base64Display.html)

`Base64Display````
use base64::{display::Base64Display, engine::general_purpose::STANDARD};
let value = Base64Display::new(b"\0\x01\x02\x03", &STANDARD);
assert_eq!("base64: AAECAw==", format!("base64: {}", value));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

If length calculations result in overflowing `usize`, a panic will result.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use engine::`- [Engine](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html);

# indexmap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/indexmap/^2/

## Expand description

[ IndexMap](https://docs.rs/map/struct.IndexMap.html) is a hash table where the iteration order of the key-value
pairs is independent of the hash values of the keys.

[ IndexSet](https://docs.rs/set/struct.IndexSet.html) is a corresponding hash set using the same implementation and
with similar properties.

[§](https://docs.rs#highlights)Highlights

[ IndexMap](https://docs.rs/map/struct.IndexMap.html) and

[are drop-in compatible with the std](https://docs.rs/set/struct.IndexSet.html)

`IndexSet``HashMap`
and `HashSet`, but they also have some features of note:- The ordering semantics (see their documentation for details)
- Sorting methods and the `.pop()`
- The `Equivalent`
- The `MutableKeys``MutableValues`

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

To reduce the amount of compiled code in the crate by default, certain
features are gated behind [feature flags](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-features-section). These allow you to opt in to (or
out of) functionality. Below is a list of the features available in this
crate.

- `std`: Enables features which require the Rust standard library. For more information see the section on- `no_std`
- `rayon`: Enables parallel iteration and other parallel methods.
- `serde`: Adds implementations for- `Serialize`- `Deserialize`- `IndexMap`- `IndexSet`- `IndexMap`- `map::serde_seq`
- `arbitrary`: Adds implementations for the- `arbitrary::Arbitrary`- `IndexMap`- `IndexSet`
- `quickcheck`: Adds implementations for the- `quickcheck::Arbitrary`- `IndexMap`- `IndexSet`
- `borsh`(- **deprecated**): Adds implementations for- `BorshSerialize`- `BorshDeserialize`- `IndexMap`- `IndexSet`- `borsh`- `indexmap`,- `borsh v1.5.6`added an- `indexmap`feature that should be used instead of enabling the feature here.

*Note: only the  std feature is enabled by default.*

[§](https://docs.rs#alternate-hashers)Alternate Hashers

[ IndexMap](https://docs.rs/map/struct.IndexMap.html) and

[have a default hasher type](https://docs.rs/set/struct.IndexSet.html)

`IndexSet`[, just like the standard](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/hash/random/struct.RandomState.html)

`S = RandomState``HashMap` and `HashSet`, which is resistant to
HashDoS attacks but not the most performant. Type aliases can make it easier
to use alternate hashers:```
use fnv::FnvBuildHasher;
use indexmap::{IndexMap, IndexSet};
type FnvIndexMap<K, V> = IndexMap<K, V, FnvBuildHasher>;
type FnvIndexSet<T> = IndexSet<T, FnvBuildHasher>;
let std: IndexSet<i32> = (0..100).collect();
let fnv: FnvIndexSet<i32> = (0..100).collect();
assert_eq!(std, fnv);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#rust-version)Rust Version

This version of indexmap requires Rust 1.85 or later.

The indexmap 2.x release series will use a carefully considered version upgrade policy, where in a later 2.x version, we will raise the minimum required Rust version.

[§](https://docs.rs#no-standard-library-targets)No Standard Library Targets

This crate supports being built without `std`, requiring `alloc` instead.
This is chosen by disabling the default “std” cargo feature, by adding
`default-features = false` to your dependency specification.

- Creating maps and sets using `new``with_capacity``std`. Use methods`IndexMap::default``with_hasher``with_capacity_and_hasher``twox-hash`.
- Macros `indexmap!``indexset!``std`. Use the macros`indexmap_with_default!``indexset_with_default!`

# krishiv_ivm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-ivm/=0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/

## Expand description

Incremental View Maintenance (IVM) engine for Krishiv.

`IncrementalFlow` is the primary API: register views, feed source deltas,
call `step_datafusion()` each tick, and subscribe to output `DeltaBatch`es.

# krishiv_state - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-state/=0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/

## Expand description

Public facade for `krishiv-state`.

Keyed state API with RocksDB backend for both ephemeral (tests/dev) and durable (file-backed) state storage.

State must be accessed only within `process_batch` or
`flush_triggered_windows` on the executor operator loop — never from
timer callbacks.

# object_store - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/object_store/^0.13.2/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#object_store)object_store

This crate provides a uniform API for interacting with object
storage services and local files via the [ ObjectStore](https://docs.rs/trait.ObjectStore.html)
trait.

Using this crate, the same binary and code can run in multiple clouds and local test environments, via a simple runtime configuration change.

[§](https://docs.rs#highlights)Highlights

-
A high-performance async API focused on providing a consistent interface mirroring that of object stores such as [S3](https://aws.amazon.com/s3/)
-
Production quality, leading this crate to be used in large scale production systems, such as [crates.io](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates.io)and [InfluxDB IOx]
-
Support for advanced functionality, including atomic, conditional reads and writes, vectored IO, bulk deletion, and more…
-
Stable and predictable governance via the [Apache Arrow](https://arrow.apache.org/)project
-
Small dependency footprint, depending on only a small number of common crates

Originally developed by [InfluxData](https://www.influxdata.com/) and subsequently donated
to [Apache Arrow](https://arrow.apache.org/).

[§](https://docs.rs#apis)APIs

- `ObjectStore`
- `ObjectStoreExt`- *New in 0.13.0*) Extension trait with additional convenience methods

[§](https://docs.rs#available-objectstore-implementations)Available `ObjectStore`

`ObjectStore`By default, this crate provides the following implementations:

- Memory: `InMemory`

Feature flags are used to enable support for other implementations:

- Local filesystem: `LocalFileSystem`
- `gcp`- [Google Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/)support. See- `GoogleCloudStorageBuilder`
- `aws`- [Amazon S3](https://aws.amazon.com/s3/). See- `AmazonS3Builder`
- `azure`- [Azure Blob Storage](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-gb/services/storage/blobs/). See- `MicrosoftAzureBuilder`
- `http`- [HTTP/WebDAV Storage](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2518). See- `HttpBuilder`

[§](https://docs.rs#why-not-a-filesystem-interface)Why not a Filesystem Interface?

The [ ObjectStore](https://docs.rs/trait.ObjectStore.html) interface is designed to mirror the APIs
of object stores and

*not*filesystems, and thus has stateless APIs instead of cursor based interfaces such as

[or](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Read.html)

`Read`[available in filesystems.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Seek.html)

`Seek`This design provides the following advantages:

- All operations are atomic, and readers cannot observe partial and/or failed writes
- Methods map directly to object store APIs, providing both efficiency and predictability
- Abstracts away filesystem and operating system specific quirks, ensuring portability
- Allows for functionality not native to filesystems, such as operation preconditions and atomic multipart uploads

This crate does provide [ BufReader](https://docs.rs/buffered/struct.BufReader.html) and

[adapters which provide a more filesystem-like API for working with the](https://docs.rs/buffered/struct.BufWriter.html)

`BufWriter`[trait, however, they should be used with care](https://docs.rs/trait.ObjectStore.html)

`ObjectStore`[§](https://docs.rs#adapters)Adapters

[ ObjectStore](https://docs.rs/trait.ObjectStore.html) instances can be composed with various adapters
which add additional functionality:

- Rate Throttling: `ThrottleConfig`
- Concurrent Request Limit: `LimitStore`

[§](https://docs.rs#configuration-system)Configuration System

This crate provides a configuration system inspired by the APIs exposed by [fsspec](https://filesystem-spec.readthedocs.io/en/latest/api.html#fsspec.filesystem),
[PyArrow FileSystem](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/python/generated/pyarrow.fs.FileSystem.html#pyarrow.fs.FileSystem.from_uri), and [Hadoop FileSystem](https://hadoop.apache.org/docs/r3.0.0/api/org/apache/hadoop/fs/FileSystem.html#get-java.net.URI-org.apache.hadoop.conf.Configuration-), allowing creating a [ DynObjectStore](https://docs.rs/type.DynObjectStore.html)
from a URL and an optional list of key value pairs. This provides a flexible interface
to support a wide variety of user-defined store configurations, with minimal additional
application complexity.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Can manually create a specific store variant using the appropriate builder
let store: AmazonS3 = AmazonS3Builder::from_env()
    .with_bucket_name("my-bucket").build().unwrap();
// Alternatively can create an ObjectStore from an S3 URL
let url = Url::parse("s3://bucket/path").unwrap();
let (store, path) = parse_url(&url).unwrap();
assert_eq!(path.as_ref(), "path");
// Potentially with additional options
let (store, path) = parse_url_opts(&url, vec![("aws_access_key_id", "...")]).unwrap();
// Or with URLs that encode the bucket name in the URL path
let url = Url::parse("https://ACCOUNT_ID.r2.cloudflarestorage.com/bucket/path").unwrap();
let (store, path) = parse_url(&url).unwrap();
assert_eq!(path.as_ref(), "path");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#list-objects)List objects

Use the [ ObjectStore::list](https://docs.rs/trait.ObjectStore.html#tymethod.list) method to iterate over objects in
remote storage or files in the local filesystem:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// create an ObjectStore
let object_store: Arc<dyn ObjectStore> = get_object_store();
// Recursively list all files below the 'data' path.
// 1. On AWS S3 this would be the 'data/' prefix
// 2. On a local filesystem, this would be the 'data' directory
let prefix = Path::from("data");
// Get an `async` stream of Metadata objects:
let mut list_stream = object_store.list(Some(&prefix));
// Print a line about each object
while let Some(meta) = list_stream.next().await.transpose().unwrap() {
    println!("Name: {}, size: {}", meta.location, meta.size);
}
```
Which will print out something like the following:

```
Name: data/file01.parquet, size: 112832
Name: data/file02.parquet, size: 143119
Name: data/child/file03.parquet, size: 100
...
```
[§](https://docs.rs#fetch-objects)Fetch objects

Use the [ ObjectStoreExt::get](https://docs.rs/trait.ObjectStoreExt.html#tymethod.get) /

[method to fetch the data bytes from remote storage or files in the local filesystem as a stream.](https://docs.rs/trait.ObjectStore.html#tymethod.get_opts)

`ObjectStore::get_opts`[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Create an ObjectStore
let object_store: Arc<dyn ObjectStore> = get_object_store();
// Retrieve a specific file
let path = Path::from("data/file01.parquet");
// Fetch just the file metadata
let meta = object_store.head(&path).await.unwrap();
println!("{meta:?}");
// Fetch the object including metadata
let result: GetResult = object_store.get(&path).await.unwrap();
assert_eq!(result.meta, meta);
// Buffer the entire object in memory
let object: Bytes = result.bytes().await.unwrap();
assert_eq!(object.len() as u64, meta.size);
// Alternatively stream the bytes from object storage
let stream = object_store.get(&path).await.unwrap().into_stream();
// Count the '0's using `try_fold` from `TryStreamExt` trait
let num_zeros = stream
    .try_fold(0, |acc, bytes| async move {
        Ok(acc + bytes.iter().filter(|b| **b == 0).count())
    }).await.unwrap();
println!("Num zeros in {} is {}", path, num_zeros);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#put-object)Put Object

Use the [ ObjectStoreExt::put](https://docs.rs/trait.ObjectStoreExt.html#tymethod.put) method to atomically write data.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let object_store: Arc<dyn ObjectStore> = get_object_store();
let path = Path::from("data/file1");
let payload = PutPayload::from_static(b"hello");
object_store.put(&path, payload).await.unwrap();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#multipart-upload)Multipart Upload

Use the [ ObjectStoreExt::put_multipart](https://docs.rs/trait.ObjectStoreExt.html#tymethod.put_multipart) /

[method to atomically write a large amount of data](https://docs.rs/trait.ObjectStore.html#tymethod.put_multipart_opts)

`ObjectStore::put_multipart_opts`[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let object_store: Arc<dyn ObjectStore> = get_object_store();
let path = Path::from("data/large_file");
let upload =  object_store.put_multipart(&path).await.unwrap();
let mut write = WriteMultipart::new(upload);
write.write(b"hello");
write.finish().await.unwrap();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#vectored-read)Vectored Read

A common pattern, especially when reading structured datasets, is to need to fetch multiple, potentially non-contiguous, ranges of a particular object.

[ ObjectStore::get_ranges](https://docs.rs/trait.ObjectStore.html#method.get_ranges) provides an efficient way to perform such vectored IO, and will
automatically coalesce adjacent ranges into an appropriate number of parallel requests.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let object_store: Arc<dyn ObjectStore> = get_object_store();
let path = Path::from("data/large_file");
let ranges = object_store.get_ranges(&path, &[90..100, 400..600, 0..10]).await.unwrap();
assert_eq!(ranges.len(), 3);
assert_eq!(ranges[0].len(), 10);
```
To retrieve ranges from a versioned object, use [ ObjectStore::get_opts](https://docs.rs/trait.ObjectStore.html#tymethod.get_opts) by specifying the range in the

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.GetOptions.html)

`GetOptions`[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let object_store: Arc<dyn ObjectStore> = get_object_store();
let path = Path::from("data/large_file");
let ranges = vec![90..100, 400..600, 0..10];
for range in ranges {
    let opts = GetOptions::default().with_range(Some(range));
    let data = object_store.get_opts(&path, opts).await.unwrap();
    // Do something with the data
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#vectored-write)Vectored Write

When writing data it is often the case that the size of the output is not known ahead of time.

A common approach to handling this is to bump-allocate a `Vec`, whereby the underlying
allocation is repeatedly reallocated, each time doubling the capacity. The performance of
this is suboptimal as reallocating memory will often involve copying it to a new location.

Fortunately, as [ PutPayload](https://docs.rs/struct.PutPayload.html) does not require memory regions to be contiguous, it is
possible to instead allocate memory in chunks and avoid bump allocating.

[encapsulates this approach](https://docs.rs/struct.PutPayloadMut.html)

`PutPayloadMut`[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let object_store: Arc<dyn ObjectStore> = get_object_store();
let path = Path::from("data/large_file");
let mut buffer = PutPayloadMut::new().with_block_size(8192);
for _ in 0..22 {
    buffer.extend_from_slice(&[0; 1024]);
}
let payload = buffer.freeze();
// Payload consists of 3 separate 8KB allocations
assert_eq!(payload.as_ref().len(), 3);
assert_eq!(payload.as_ref()[0].len(), 8192);
assert_eq!(payload.as_ref()[1].len(), 8192);
assert_eq!(payload.as_ref()[2].len(), 6144);
object_store.put(&path, payload).await.unwrap();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#conditional-fetch)Conditional Fetch

More complex object retrieval can be supported by [ ObjectStore::get_opts](https://docs.rs/trait.ObjectStore.html#tymethod.get_opts).

For example, efficiently refreshing a cache without re-fetching the entire object data if the object hasn’t been modified.

```
struct CacheEntry {
    /// Data returned by last request
    data: Bytes,
    /// ETag identifying the object returned by the server
    e_tag: String,
    /// Instant of last refresh
    refreshed_at: Instant,
}
/// Example cache that checks entries after 10 seconds for a new version
struct Cache {
    entries: HashMap<Path, CacheEntry>,
    store: Arc<dyn ObjectStore>,
}
impl Cache {
    pub async fn get(&mut self, path: &Path) -> Result<Bytes> {
        Ok(match self.entries.get_mut(path) {
            Some(e) => match e.refreshed_at.elapsed() < Duration::from_secs(10) {
                true => e.data.clone(), // Return cached data
                false => { // Check if remote version has changed
                    let opts = GetOptions::new().with_if_none_match(Some(e.e_tag.clone()));
                    match self.store.get_opts(&path, opts).await {
                        Ok(d) => e.data = d.bytes().await?,
                        Err(Error::NotModified { .. }) => {} // Data has not changed
                        Err(e) => return Err(e),
                    };
                    e.refreshed_at = Instant::now();
                    e.data.clone()
                }
            },
            None => { // Not cached, fetch data
                let get = self.store.get(&path).await?;
                let e_tag = get.meta.e_tag.clone();
                let data = get.bytes().await?;
                if let Some(e_tag) = e_tag {
                    let entry = CacheEntry {
                        e_tag,
                        data: data.clone(),
                        refreshed_at: Instant::now(),
                    };
                    self.entries.insert(path.clone(), entry);
                }
                data
            }
        })
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#conditional-put)Conditional Put

The default behaviour when writing data is to upsert any existing object at the given path,
overwriting any previous value. More complex behaviours can be achieved using [ PutMode](https://docs.rs/enum.PutMode.html), and
can be used to build

[Optimistic Concurrency Control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optimistic_concurrency_control)based transactions. This facilitates building metadata catalogs, such as

[Apache Iceberg](https://iceberg.apache.org/)or

[Delta Lake](https://delta.io/), directly on top of object storage, without relying on a separate DBMS.

```
let store = get_object_store();
let path = Path::from("test");
// Perform a conditional update on path
loop {
    // Perform get request
    let r = store.get(&path).await.unwrap();
    // Save version information fetched
    let version = UpdateVersion {
        e_tag: r.meta.e_tag.clone(),
        version: r.meta.version.clone(),
    };
    // Compute new version of object contents
    let new = do_update(r.bytes().await.unwrap());
    // Attempt to commit transaction
    match store.put_opts(&path, new.into(), PutMode::Update(version).into()).await {
        Ok(_) => break, // Successfully committed
        Err(Error::Precondition { .. }) => continue, // Object has changed, try again
        Err(e) => panic!("{e}")
    }
}
```

Stores that use HTTPS/TLS (this is true for most cloud stores) can choose the source of their [CA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certificate_authority)

[ rustls-native-certs](https://crates.io/crates/rustls-native-certs/)). The

`tls-webpki-roots` feature switch can be used to also bundle Mozilla’s
root certificates with the library/application (see [).](https://crates.io/crates/webpki-roots)

# reqwest - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/reqwest/^0.13.4/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#reqwest)reqwest

The `reqwest` crate provides a convenient, higher-level HTTP
[ Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html).

It handles many of the things that most people just expect an HTTP client to do for them.

- Async and [blocking](https://docs.rs/blocking/index.html)Clients
- Plain bodies, [JSON](https://docs.rs#json),[urlencoded](https://docs.rs#forms),[multipart](https://docs.rs/multipart/index.html)
- Customizable [redirect policy](https://docs.rs#redirect-policies)
- HTTP [Proxies](https://docs.rs#proxies)
- Uses [TLS](https://docs.rs#tls)by default
- Cookies

The [ reqwest::Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html) is asynchronous (requiring Tokio). For
applications wishing  to only make a few HTTP requests, the

[API may be more convenient.](https://docs.rs/blocking/index.html)

`reqwest::blocking`Additional learning resources include:

[§](https://docs.rs#commercial-support)Commercial Support

For private advice, support, reviews, access to the maintainer, and the
like, reach out for [commercial support](https://seanmonstar.com/sponsor).

[§](https://docs.rs#making-a-get-request)Making a GET request

For a single request, you can use the [ get](https://docs.rs/fn.get.html) shortcut method.

```
let body = reqwest::get("https://www.rust-lang.org")
    .await?
    .text()
    .await?;
println!("body = {body:?}");
```
**NOTE**: If you plan to perform multiple requests, it is best to create a
[ Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html) and reuse it, taking advantage of keep-alive connection
pooling.

[§](https://docs.rs#making-post-requests-or-setting-request-bodies)Making POST requests (or setting request bodies)

There are several ways you can set the body of a request. The basic one is
by using the `body()` method of a [ RequestBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.RequestBuilder.html). This lets you set the
exact raw bytes of what the body should be. It accepts various types,
including

`String` and `Vec<u8>`. If you wish to pass a custom
type, you can use the `reqwest::Body` constructors.```
let client = reqwest::Client::new();
let res = client.post("http://httpbin.org/post")
    .body("the exact body that is sent")
    .send()
    .await?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#forms)Forms

It’s very common to want to send form data in a request body. This can be done with any type that can be serialized into form data.

This can be an array of tuples, or a `HashMap`, or a custom type that
implements [ Serialize](http://serde.rs).

The feature `form` is required.

```
// This will POST a body of `foo=bar&baz=quux`
let params = [("foo", "bar"), ("baz", "quux")];
let client = reqwest::Client::new();
let res = client.post("http://httpbin.org/post")
    .form(¶ms)
    .send()
    .await?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#json)JSON

There is also a `json` method helper on the [ RequestBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.RequestBuilder.html) that works in
a similar fashion the

`form` method. It can take any value that can be
serialized into JSON.The feature `json` is required.

```
// This will POST a body of `{"lang":"rust","body":"json"}`
let mut map = HashMap::new();
map.insert("lang", "rust");
map.insert("body", "json");
let client = reqwest::Client::new();
let res = client.post("http://httpbin.org/post")
    .json(&map)
    .send()
    .await?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#redirect-policies)Redirect Policies

By default, a `Client` will automatically handle HTTP redirects, having a
maximum redirect chain of 10 hops. To customize this behavior, a
[ redirect::Policy](https://docs.rs/redirect/index.html) can be used with a

`ClientBuilder`.[§](https://docs.rs#cookies)Cookies

The automatic storing and sending of session cookies can be enabled with
the [ cookie_store](https://docs.rs/struct.ClientBuilder.html#method.cookie_store) method on

`ClientBuilder`.[§](https://docs.rs#proxies)Proxies

**NOTE**: System proxies are enabled by default.

System proxies look in environment variables to set HTTP or HTTPS proxies.

`HTTP_PROXY` or `http_proxy` provide HTTP proxies for HTTP connections while
`HTTPS_PROXY` or `https_proxy` provide HTTPS proxies for HTTPS connections.
`ALL_PROXY` or `all_proxy` provide proxies for both HTTP and HTTPS connections.
If both the all proxy and HTTP or HTTPS proxy variables are set the more specific
HTTP or HTTPS proxies take precedence.

These can be overwritten by adding a [ Proxy](https://docs.rs/struct.Proxy.html) to

`ClientBuilder`
i.e. `let proxy = reqwest::Proxy::http("https://secure.example")?;`
or disabled by calling `ClientBuilder::no_proxy()`.`socks` feature is required if you have configured socks proxy like this:

`export https_proxy=socks5://127.0.0.1:1086`[§](https://docs.rs#tls)TLS

A `Client` will use transport layer security (TLS) by default to connect to
HTTPS destinations.

- Additional server certificates can be configured on a `ClientBuilder`with the`Certificate`
- Client certificates can be added to a `ClientBuilder`with the`Identity`
- Various parts of TLS can also be configured or even disabled on the
`ClientBuilder`.

See more details in the [ tls](https://docs.rs/tls/index.html) module.

[§](https://docs.rs#wasm)WASM

The Client implementation automatically switches to the WASM one when the target_arch is wasm32,
the usage is basically the same as the async api. Some of the features are disabled in wasm
: [ tls](https://docs.rs/tls/index.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/cookie/index.html)

`cookie`[, as well as various](https://docs.rs/blocking/index.html)

`blocking``ClientBuilder` methods such as `timeout()` and `connector_layer()`.TLS and cookies are provided through the browser environment, so reqwest can issue TLS requests with cookies, but has limited configuration.

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional Features

The following are a list of [Cargo features](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-features-section) that can be
enabled or disabled:

- **http2**- *(enabled by default)*: Enables HTTP/2 support.
- **default-tls**- *(enabled by default)*: Provides TLS support to connect over HTTPS.
- **rustls**: Enables TLS functionality provided by- `rustls`.
- **rustls-no-provider**: Enables TLS provided by- `rustls`without specifying a crypto provider.
- **native-tls**: Enables TLS functionality provided by- `native-tls`.
- **native-tls-vendored**: Enables the- `vendored`feature of- `native-tls`.
- **native-tls-no-alpn**: Enables- `native-tls`without its- `alpn`feature.
- **native-tls-vendored-no-alpn**: Enables- `native-tls-vendored`without its- `alpn`feature.
- **blocking**: Provides the- [blocking](https://docs.rs/blocking/index.html)client API.
- **charset**- *(enabled by default)*: Improved support for decoding text.
- **cookies**: Provides cookie session support.
- **gzip**: Provides response body gzip decompression.
- **brotli**: Provides response body brotli decompression.
- **zstd**: Provides response body zstd decompression.
- **deflate**: Provides response body deflate decompression.
- **query**: Provides query parameter serialization.
- **form**: Provides form data serialization.
- **json**: Provides serialization and deserialization for JSON bodies.
- **multipart**: Provides functionality for multipart forms.
- **stream**: Adds support for- `futures::Stream`.
- **socks**: Provides SOCKS5 proxy support.
- **hickory-dns**: Enables a hickory-dns async resolver instead of default threadpool using- `getaddrinfo`.
- **system-proxy**- *(enabled by default)*: Use Windows and macOS system proxy settings automatically.

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable Features

Some feature flags require additional opt-in by the application, by setting
a `reqwest_unstable` flag.

- **http3**- *(unstable)*: Enables support for sending HTTP/3 requests.

These features are unstable, and experimental. Details about them may be changed in patch releases.

You can pass such a flag to the compiler via `.cargo/config`, or
environment variables, such as:

`RUSTFLAGS="--cfg reqwest_unstable" cargo build`[§](https://docs.rs#sponsors)Sponsors

# tokio_stream - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tokio-stream/^0.1.18/

## Expand description

Stream utilities for Tokio.

A `Stream` is an asynchronous sequence of values. It can be thought of as
an asynchronous version of the standard library’s `Iterator` trait.

This crate provides helpers to work with them. For examples of usage and a more in-depth
description of streams you can also refer to the [streams
tutorial](https://tokio.rs/tokio/tutorial/streams) on the tokio website.

[§](https://docs.rs#iterating-over-a-stream)Iterating over a Stream

Due to similarities with the standard library’s `Iterator` trait, some new
users may assume that they can use `for in` syntax to iterate over a
`Stream`, but this is unfortunately not possible. Instead, you can use a
`while let` loop as follows:

```
use tokio_stream::{self as stream, StreamExt};
let mut stream = stream::iter(vec![0, 1, 2]);
while let Some(value) = stream.next().await {
    println!("Got {}", value);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#returning-a-stream-from-a-function)Returning a Stream from a function

A common way to stream values from a function is to pass in the sender
half of a channel and use the receiver as the stream. This requires awaiting
both futures to ensure progress is made. Another alternative is the
[async-stream](https://docs.rs/async-stream) crate, which contains macros that provide a `yield` keyword
and allow you to return an `impl Stream`.

[§](https://docs.rs#conversion-to-and-from-asyncreadasyncwrite)Conversion to and from `AsyncRead`/`AsyncWrite`

It is often desirable to convert a `Stream` into an [ AsyncRead](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/io/trait.AsyncRead.html),
especially when dealing with plaintext formats streamed over the network.
The opposite conversion from an

[into a](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/io/trait.AsyncRead.html)

`AsyncRead``Stream` is also
another commonly required feature. To enable these conversions,
[provides the](https://docs.rs/tokio-util/latest/tokio_util/codec/index.html)

`tokio-util`[and](https://docs.rs/tokio-util/latest/tokio_util/io/struct.StreamReader.html)

`StreamReader`[types when the io feature is enabled.](https://docs.rs/tokio-util/latest/tokio_util/io/struct.ReaderStream.html)

`ReaderStream`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use futures_core::`- [Stream](https://docs.rs/futures-core/0.3.32/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/futures_core/stream/trait.Stream.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [adapters](https://docs.rs/adapters/index.html)
- Adapters for `Stream``StreamExt`
- [wrappers](https://docs.rs/wrappers/index.html)
- Wrappers for Tokio types that implement `Stream`.

# tonic - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tonic/^0.14.6/

## Expand description

A Rust implementation of [gRPC](https://grpc.io), a high performance, open source, general
RPC framework that puts mobile and HTTP/2 first.

[ tonic](https://github.com/hyperium/tonic) is a gRPC over HTTP/2 implementation focused on

**high performance**,

**interoperability**, and

**flexibility**. This library was created to have first class support of async/await and to act as a core building block for production systems written in Rust.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Examples can be found in the [ tonic-examples](https://github.com/hyperium/tonic/tree/master/examples) crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting Started

Follow the instructions in the [ tonic-build](https://docs.rs/tonic-build) crate documentation.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

- `transport`: Enables the fully featured, batteries included client and server implementation based on- `hyper`- `tower`- `tokio`- `server`and- `channel`features. Enabled by default.
- `server`: Enables just the full featured server portion of the- `transport`feature.
- `channel`: Enables just the full featured channel portion of the- `transport`feature.
- `router`: Enables the- `axum`
- `codegen`: Enables all the required exports and optional dependencies required for- `tonic-build`
- `tls-ring`: Enables the- `rustls`- `transport`feature using the- `ring`
- `tls-aws-lc`: Enables the- `rustls`- `transport`feature using the- `aws-lc-rs`
- `tls-native-roots`: Adds system trust roots to- `rustls`- `rustls-native-certs`
- `tls-webpki-roots`: Add the standard trust roots from the- `webpki-roots`- `rustls`-based gRPC clients. Not enabled by default.
- `tls-connect-info`: Adds additional implementations of- `Connected`- `tls-*`features are enabled. This feature is useful for when trying to use a custom TLS connector with- `connect_with_connector`without enabling any- `tls-*`features.
- `gzip`: Enables compressing requests, responses, and streams. Depends on- `flate2`
- `deflate`: Enables compressing requests, responses, and streams. Depends on- `flate2`
- `zstd`: Enables compressing requests, responses, and streams. Depends on- `zstd`

[§](https://docs.rs#structure)Structure

[§](https://docs.rs#generic-implementation)Generic implementation

The main goal of [ tonic](https://github.com/hyperium/tonic) is to provide a generic gRPC implementation over HTTP/2
framing. This means at the lowest level this library provides the ability to use
a generic HTTP/2 implementation with different types of gRPC encodings formats. Generally,
some form of codegen should be used instead of interacting directly with the items in

[and](https://docs.rs/client/index.html)

`client`[.](https://docs.rs/transport/struct.Server.html)

`server`[§](https://docs.rs#transport)Transport

The [ transport](https://docs.rs/transport/index.html) module contains a fully featured HTTP/2.0

[(gRPC terminology) and](https://docs.rs/transport/struct.Channel.html)

`Channel`[. These implementations are built on top of](https://docs.rs/transport/struct.Server.html)

`Server`[,](https://docs.rs/tokio)

`tokio`[and](https://docs.rs/hyper)

`hyper`[. It also provides many of the features that the core gRPC libraries provide such as load balancing, tls, timeouts, and many more. This implementation can also be used as a reference implementation to build even more feature rich clients and servers. This module also provides the ability to enable TLS using](https://docs.rs/tower)

`tower`[, via the](https://docs.rs/rustls)

`rustls``tls` feature flag.[§](https://docs.rs#code-generated-clientserver-configuration)Code generated client/server configuration

[§](https://docs.rs#max-message-size)Max Message Size

Currently, both servers and clients can be configured to set the max message encoding and
decoding size. This will ensure that an incoming gRPC message will not exhaust the systems
memory. By default, the decoding message limit is `4MB` and the encoding limit is `usize::MAX`.

# twox_hash - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/twox-hash/^2.1/

## Expand description

A Rust implementation of the [xxHash](https://github.com/Cyan4973/xxHash) algorithm.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

These examples use [ XxHash64](https://docs.rs/xxhash64/struct.Hasher.html) but the same ideas can be
used for

[,](https://docs.rs/xxhash32/struct.Hasher.html)

`XxHash32`[, or](https://docs.rs/xxhash3_64/struct.Hasher.html)

`XxHash3_64`[.](https://docs.rs/xxhash3_128/struct.Hasher.html)

`XxHash3_128`[§](https://docs.rs#hashing-arbitrary-data)Hashing arbitrary data

[§](https://docs.rs#when-all-the-data-is-available-at-once)When all the data is available at once

```
use twox_hash::XxHash64;
let seed = 1234;
let hash = XxHash64::oneshot(seed, b"some bytes");
assert_eq!(0xeab5_5659_a496_d78b, hash);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#when-the-data-is-streaming)When the data is streaming

```
use std::hash::Hasher as _;
use twox_hash::XxHash64;
let seed = 1234;
let mut hasher = XxHash64::with_seed(seed);
hasher.write(b"some");
hasher.write(b" ");
hasher.write(b"bytes");
let hash = hasher.finish();
assert_eq!(0xeab5_5659_a496_d78b, hash);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#with-a-default-seed)With a default seed

```
use std::{collections::HashMap, hash::BuildHasherDefault};
use twox_hash::XxHash64;
let mut hash = HashMap::<_, _, BuildHasherDefault<XxHash64>>::default();
hash.insert(42, "the answer");
assert_eq!(hash.get(&42), Some(&"the answer"));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#with-a-random-seed)With a random seed

```
use std::collections::HashMap;
use twox_hash::xxhash64;
let mut hash = HashMap::<_, _, xxhash64::RandomState>::default();
hash.insert(42, "the answer");
assert_eq!(hash.get(&42), Some(&"the answer"));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#with-a-fixed-seed)With a fixed seed

```
use std::collections::HashMap;
use twox_hash::xxhash64;
let mut hash = HashMap::with_hasher(xxhash64::State::with_seed(0xdead_cafe));
hash.insert(42, "the answer");
assert_eq!(hash.get(&42), Some(&"the answer"));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

| name | description |
|---|---|
| xxhash32 | Include the algorithm`XxHash32` |
| xxhash64 | Include the algorithm`XxHash64` |
| xxhash3_64 | Include the algorithm`XxHash3_64` |
| xxhash3_128 | Include the algorithm`XxHash3_128` |
| random | Create random instances of the hashers |
| serialize | Serialize and deserialize hasher state with Serde |
| std | Use the Rust standard library. Enable this if you want SIMD support in or`XxHash3_64``XxHash3_128` |
| alloc | Use the Rust allocator library. Enable this if you want to create or`XxHash3_64`with dynamic secrets`XxHash3_128` |

See benchmarks in the [comparison](https://github.com/shepmaster/twox-hash/tree/main/comparison) README.

# parquet - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/parquet/^58.3.0/

## Expand description

This crate contains the official Native Rust implementation of
[Apache Parquet](https://parquet.apache.org/), part of
the [Apache Arrow](https://arrow.apache.org/) project.
The crate provides a number of APIs to read and write Parquet files,
covering a range of use cases.

Please see the [parquet crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/parquet)
page for feature flags and tips to improve performance.

[§](https://docs.rs#format-overview)Format Overview

Parquet is a columnar format, which means that unlike row formats like [CSV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comma-separated_values), values are
iterated along columns instead of rows. Parquet is similar in spirit to [Arrow](https://docs.rs/arrow/latest/arrow/index.html), but
focuses on storage efficiency whereas Arrow prioritizes compute efficiency.

Parquet files are partitioned for scalability. Each file contains metadata, along with zero or more “row groups”, each row group containing one or more columns. The APIs in this crate reflect this structure.

Data in Parquet files is strongly typed and differentiates between logical
and physical types (see [ schema](https://docs.rs/schema/index.html)). In addition, Parquet files may contain
other metadata, such as statistics, which can be used to optimize reading
(see

[). For more details about the Parquet format itself, see the](https://docs.rs/file/metadata/index.html)

`file::metadata`[Parquet spec](https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/blob/master/README.md#file-format)

[§](https://docs.rs#apis)APIs

This crate exposes a number of APIs for different use-cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#metadata-and-schema)Metadata and Schema

The [ schema](https://docs.rs/schema/index.html) module provides APIs to work with Parquet schemas. The

[module provides APIs to work with Parquet metadata.](https://docs.rs/file/metadata/index.html)

`file::metadata`[§](https://docs.rs#reading-and-writing-arrow-arrow-feature)Reading and Writing Arrow (`arrow` feature)

The [ arrow](https://docs.rs/arrow/index.html) module supports reading and writing Parquet data to/from
Arrow

[es. Using Arrow is simple and performant, and allows workloads to leverage the wide range of data transforms provided by the](https://docs.rs/arrow/latest/arrow/array/struct.RecordBatch.html)

`RecordBatch`[arrow](https://docs.rs/arrow/latest/arrow/index.html)crate, and by the ecosystem of

[Arrow](https://docs.rs/arrow/latest/arrow/index.html)compatible systems.

Most users will use [ ArrowWriter](https://docs.rs/arrow/arrow_writer/struct.ArrowWriter.html) for writing and

[for reading from synchronous IO sources such as files or in-memory buffers.](https://docs.rs/arrow/arrow_reader/type.ParquetRecordBatchReaderBuilder.html)

`ParquetRecordBatchReaderBuilder`Lower level APIs include

- `ParquetPushDecoder`
- `ArrowColumnWriter`
- `RowFilter`

[§](https://docs.rs#experimental-content-defined-chunking)EXPERIMENTAL: Content-Defined Chunking

[ ArrowWriter](https://docs.rs/arrow/arrow_writer/struct.ArrowWriter.html) supports content-defined chunking (CDC), which creates data page
boundaries based on content rather than fixed sizes. CDC enables efficient
deduplication in content-addressable storage (CAS) systems: when the same data
appears in successive file versions, it will produce identical byte sequences that
CAS backends can deduplicate.

Enable CDC via [ WriterProperties](https://docs.rs/file/properties/struct.WriterProperties.html):

```
let props = WriterProperties::builder()
    .set_content_defined_chunking(Some(CdcOptions::default()))
    .build();
```
See [ CdcOptions](https://docs.rs/file/properties/struct.CdcOptions.html) for chunk size and normalization parameters.

[§](https://docs.rs#async-reading-and-writing-arrow-arrow-feature--async-feature)`async` Reading and Writing Arrow (`arrow` feature + `async` feature)

The [ async_reader](https://docs.rs/arrow/async_reader/index.html) and

[modules provide async APIs to read and write](https://docs.rs/arrow/async_writer/index.html)

`async_writer`[es asynchronously.](https://docs.rs/arrow/latest/arrow/array/struct.RecordBatch.html)

`RecordBatch`Most users will use [ AsyncArrowWriter](https://docs.rs/arrow/async_writer/struct.AsyncArrowWriter.html) for writing and

[for reading. When the](https://docs.rs/arrow/async_reader/type.ParquetRecordBatchStreamBuilder.html)

`ParquetRecordBatchStreamBuilder``object_store` feature is enabled, [provides efficient integration with object storage services such as S3 via the](https://docs.rs/arrow/async_reader/struct.ParquetObjectReader.html)

`ParquetObjectReader`[object_store](https://docs.rs/object_store/latest/object_store/)crate, automatically optimizing IO based on any predicates or projections provided.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant-logical-type-variant_experimental-feature)Variant Logical Type (`variant_experimental` feature)

The [ variant](https://docs.rs/variant/index.html) module supports reading and writing Parquet files
with the

[Variant Binary Encoding](https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/blob/master/VariantEncoding.md)logical type, which can represent semi-structured data such as JSON efficiently.

[§](https://docs.rs#readwrite-parquet-directly)Read/Write Parquet Directly

Workloads needing finer-grained control, or to avoid a dependence on arrow,
can use the APIs in [ file](https://docs.rs/file/index.html) directly. These APIs  are harder to use
as they directly use the underlying Parquet data model, and require knowledge
of the Parquet format, including the details of

[Dremel](https://research.google/pubs/pub36632/)record shredding and

[Logical Types](https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/blob/master/LogicalTypes.md).

# tempfile - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tempfile/^3/

## Expand description

This is a library for creating temporary files and directories that are automatically deleted when no longer referenced (i.e., on drop).

- Use `tempfile()``std::fs::File`
- Use `NamedTempFile::new()`*named*temporary file that can be referred to its path.
- Use `tempdir()`
- Use `spooled_tempfile()`

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

This crate provides several approaches to creating temporary files and directories.
[ tempfile()](https://docs.rs/fn.tempfile.html) relies on the OS to remove the temporary file once the last handle is closed.

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html)

`TempDir`[both rely on Rust destructors for cleanup.](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)

`NamedTempFile`[§](https://docs.rs#resource-leaking)Resource Leaking

`tempfile` will (almost) never fail to cleanup temporary resources. However `TempDir` and
`NamedTempFile` will fail if their destructors don’t run. This is because `tempfile` relies on
the OS to cleanup the underlying file, while `TempDir` and `NamedTempFile` rely on rust
destructors to do so. Destructors may fail to run if the process exits through an unhandled
signal interrupt (like `SIGINT`), or if the instance is declared statically (like with
[ lazy_static](https://github.com/rust-lang-nursery/lazy-static.rs/issues/62)), among other possible reasons.

[§](https://docs.rs#unexpected-file-deletion)Unexpected File Deletion

Most operating systems periodically clean up temporary files that haven’t been accessed recently
(often on the order of multiple days). This issue does not affect unnamed temporary files but
can invalidate the paths associated with named temporary files on Unix-like systems because the
temporary file can be unlinked from the filesystem while still open and in-use. See the
[temporary file cleaner](https://docs.rs#temporary-file-cleaners) section for more security implications.

[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

This section discusses security issues relevant to Unix-like operating systems that use shared temporary directories by default. Importantly, it’s not relevant for Windows or macOS as both operating systems use private per-user temporary directories by default.

Applications can mitigate the issues described below by using [ env::override_temp_dir](https://docs.rs/env/fn.override_temp_dir.html) to
change the default temporary directory but should do so if and only if default the temporary
directory (

[) is unsuitable (is world readable, world writable, managed by a temporary file cleaner, etc.).](https://docs.rs/env/fn.temp_dir.html)

`env::temp_dir`[§](https://docs.rs#temporary-file-cleaners)Temporary File Cleaners

In the presence of pathological temporary file cleaner, relying on file paths is unsafe because a temporary file cleaner could delete the temporary file which an attacker could then replace.

This isn’t an issue for [ tempfile](https://docs.rs/fn.tempfile.html) as it doesn’t rely on file paths. However,

[and temporary directories](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)

`NamedTempFile`*do*rely on file paths for

*some*operations. See the security documentation on the

[and the](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)

`NamedTempFile`[types for more information.](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html)

`TempDir`Mitigation:

- This is rarely an issue for short-lived files as temporary file cleaners usually only remove temporary files that haven’t been modified or accessed within many (10-30) days.
- Very long lived temporary files should be placed in directories not managed by temporary file cleaners.

[§](https://docs.rs#access-permissions)Access Permissions

Temporary *files* created with this library are private by default on all operating systems.
However, temporary *directories* are created with the default permissions and will therefore be
world-readable by default unless the user has changed their umask and/or default temporary
directory.

[§](https://docs.rs#denial-of-service)Denial of Service

If the file-name randomness ([ Builder::rand_bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.rand_bytes)) is too small and/or this crate is built
without the

`getrandom` feature, it may be possible for an attacker to predict the random file
names chosen by this library, preventing temporary file creation by creating temporary files
with these predicted file names. By default, this library mitigates this denial of service
attack by:- Defaulting to 6 random characters per temporary file forcing an attacker to create billions of files before random collisions are expected (at which point you probably have larger problems).
- Re-seeding the random filename generator from system randomness after 3 failed attempts to
create temporary a file (when the `getrandom`feature is enabled as it is by default on all major platforms).

[§](https://docs.rs#early-drop-pitfall)Early drop pitfall

Because `TempDir` and `NamedTempFile` rely on their destructors for cleanup, this can lead
to an unexpected early removal of the directory/file, usually when working with APIs which are
generic over `AsRef<Path>`. Consider the following example:

```
use tempfile::tempdir;
use std::process::Command;
// Create a directory inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let temp_dir = tempdir()?;
// Spawn the `touch` command inside the temporary directory and collect the exit status
// Note that `temp_dir` is **not** moved into `current_dir`, but passed as a reference
let exit_status = Command::new("touch").arg("tmp").current_dir(&temp_dir).status()?;
assert!(exit_status.success());
```
This works because a reference to `temp_dir` is passed to `current_dir`, resulting in the
destructor of `temp_dir` being run after the `Command` has finished execution. Moving the
`TempDir` into the `current_dir` call would result in the `TempDir` being converted into
an internal representation, with the original value being dropped and the directory thus
being deleted, before the command can be executed.

The `touch` command would fail with an `No such file or directory` error.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Create a temporary file and write some data into it:

```
use tempfile::tempfile;
use std::io::Write;
// Create a file inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let mut file = tempfile()?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
```
Create a named temporary file and open an independent file handle:

```
use tempfile::NamedTempFile;
use std::io::{Write, Read};
let text = "Brian was here. Briefly.";
// Create a file inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let mut file1 = NamedTempFile::new()?;
// Re-open it.
let mut file2 = file1.reopen()?;
// Write some test data to the first handle.
file1.write_all(text.as_bytes())?;
// Read the test data using the second handle.
let mut buf = String::new();
file2.read_to_string(&mut buf)?;
assert_eq!(buf, text);
```
Create a temporary directory and add a file to it:

```
use tempfile::tempdir;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Write;
// Create a directory inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let dir = tempdir()?;
let file_path = dir.path().join("my-temporary-note.txt");
let mut file = File::create(file_path)?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
// By closing the `TempDir` explicitly, we can check that it has
// been deleted successfully. If we don't close it explicitly,
// the directory will still be deleted when `dir` goes out
// of scope, but we won't know whether deleting the directory
// succeeded.
drop(file);
dir.close()?;
```

pub enum AssignmentPushOutcome {
    Enqueued,
    Duplicate,
}

## Expand description

Result of pushing an assignment into the executor inbox.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Enqueued)

### Enqueued

The assignment was queued for execution.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Duplicate)

### Duplicate

The same `(job, task, attempt)` was already received.

Create a bounded inbox with the given maximum number of queued assignments.
Pushes beyond this limit will fail with `ExecutorError::AssignmentQueueFull`.

Returns a reference to the wakeup notifier so executor slot loops can

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_executor/assignment_inbox.rs.html#155-200)#### pub fn [push_with_outcome](https://docs.rs#method.push_with_outcome)(

#### pub fn [push_with_outcome](https://docs.rs#method.push_with_outcome)(
    &self,
    assignment: [ExecutorTaskAssignment](https://docs.rs/krishiv-proto/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/krishiv_proto/task/struct.ExecutorTaskAssignment.html),
) -> [ExecutorResult](https://docs.rs/error/type.ExecutorResult.html)<[AssignmentPushOutcome](https://docs.rs/enum.AssignmentPushOutcome.html)>

Store one received assignment and report whether it was newly queued or already present.

Lock order: the `seen` set and `assignments` queue are both protected by
their own `RwLock`. We acquire `seen` *first* and hold it across the
capacity check + insert to prevent the TOCTOU race that the prior
implementation had: a duplicate `(job, task, attempt)` could observe
`seen.insert == true` and then be rejected on capacity, leaving the
`seen` set with a stale entry that blocks later legitimate re-pushes.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_executor/assignment_inbox.rs.html#222-255)#### pub fn [cancel_task](https://docs.rs#method.cancel_task)(&self, task_id: &[TaskId](https://docs.rs/krishiv-proto/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/krishiv_proto/ids/struct.TaskId.html)) -> [ExecutorResult](https://docs.rs/error/type.ExecutorResult.html)<[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_executor/assignment_inbox.rs.html#222-255)

#### pub fn [cancel_task](https://docs.rs#method.cancel_task)(&self, task_id: &[TaskId](https://docs.rs/krishiv-proto/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/krishiv_proto/ids/struct.TaskId.html)) -> [ExecutorResult](https://docs.rs/error/type.ExecutorResult.html)<[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)>

Cancel and remove queued assignments for a task id.

Also marks the task id as cancelled so the runner can skip execution even if the task has already been popped from the queue.

Lock order: `seen` → `assignments` → `cancelled_tasks`. This matches the
order used by [`push_with_outcome`] (`seen` → `assignments`), so a
concurrent `push` and `cancel_task` cannot deadlock via AB-BA. We hold
`seen`’s write-lock across the queue mutation so that no `push` can
observe a key already removed from `assignments` while still seeing it
in `seen` (which would block a legitimate re-push).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_executor/assignment_inbox.rs.html#258-264)

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidExecutorId)

### InvalidExecutorId

Executor id failed validation.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidSlots)

### InvalidSlots

Task slots must be greater than zero.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.EmptyCoordinatorEndpoint)

### EmptyCoordinatorEndpoint

Coordinator endpoint cannot be empty.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.AssignmentInboxPoisoned)

### AssignmentInboxPoisoned

The executor assignment inbox lock was poisoned.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.AssignmentQueueFull)

### AssignmentQueueFull

The assignment inbox has reached its configured capacity. This is the backpressure signal — the coordinator should slow down or the executor is overloaded / recovering.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidAssignment)

### InvalidAssignment

A received task assignment cannot be executed.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.LocalExecution)

### LocalExecution

Local stage fragment execution failed.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.StreamingNotImplemented)

### StreamingNotImplemented

A streaming task fragment was submitted but streaming execution is not available on this executor configuration.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ShufflePartitionMissing)

### ShufflePartitionMissing

An upstream shuffle partition could not be fetched because the producer’s output is no longer available (executor lost, disk failure).

This is a non-retryable failure at the consumer; the coordinator must re-schedule the producing task to regenerate the partition.

# ExecutionModel in krishiv_executor::execution_model - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-executor/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_executor/execution_model/enum.ExecutionModel.html

```
pub enum ExecutionModel {
    Batch,
    Streaming,
    DeltaBatch,
}
```
## Expand description

Execution model inferred from a plan fragment description.

This is the central dispatch point that separates batch-terminal execution (R1–R4) from streaming-continuous execution (R5+). Every call site that would otherwise string-match on the fragment prefix should use this enum.

**Batch**: the runner executes the fragment, collects output, and reports
`TaskState::Succeeded` or `TaskState::Failed`.  The task has a finite
lifetime. Optional `task_timeout_secs` applies.

**Streaming**: the runner enters a continuous operator loop and never reports
`Succeeded` while the job is running.  The task terminates only on an
explicit `Stop` signal from the coordinator or on a fatal error.
`task_timeout_secs` is *ignored* for streaming tasks because the duration
is unbounded by design.  R5.1 provides the first real streaming runner;
until then, submitting a `stream:` fragment returns
`ExecutorError::StreamingNotImplemented`.

**DeltaBatch**: one bounded tick of an IVM job. The executor processes
pending source deltas, runs the view SQL, diffs outputs, and returns each
view’s full output as task output. The executor is **stateless**: each tick
runs on a transient flow seeded from a coordinator-shipped state snapshot,
so executors remain replaceable workers. The coordinator is the single
source of truth (see `submit_distributed_ivm_step` in `krishiv-scheduler`).

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Batch)

### Batch

Task runs to completion and returns terminal output.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Streaming)

### Streaming

Task runs an unbounded loop until a `Stop` signal or fatal error.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.DeltaBatch)

### DeltaBatch

One bounded IVM tick: apply deltas, run SQL, diff, return output deltas.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

`pub trait BarrierSource: `[Send](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html) + [Sync](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sync.html) {
    // Required method
    fn [next_barrier](https://docs.rs#tymethod.next_barrier)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[CheckpointBarrier](https://docs.rs/krishiv-proto/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/krishiv_proto/wire/v1/struct.CheckpointBarrier.html)>;
}## Expand description

Abstraction over any barrier source so downstream operators can consume barriers
without being coupled to `SharedBarrierInjector` directly.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# CheckpointStateHandle in krishiv_executor::runner - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-executor/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_executor/runner/enum.CheckpointStateHandle.html

```
pub enum CheckpointStateHandle {
    Backend(
```
[Arc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/sync/struct.Arc.html)<[Mutex](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/sync/poison/mutex/struct.Mutex.html)<[Box](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/boxed/struct.Box.html)<dyn [StateBackend](https://docs.rs/krishiv-state/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/krishiv_state/backend/trait.StateBackend.html)>>>),
    ContinuousWindow([Arc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/sync/struct.Arc.html)<[Mutex](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/sync/poison/mutex/struct.Mutex.html)<[ContinuousWindowExecutor](https://docs.rs/krishiv-dataflow/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/krishiv_dataflow/continuous/struct.ContinuousWindowExecutor.html)>>),
}## Expand description

Typed access to the state a task snapshots at a checkpoint barrier and reloads at restore.

Continuous window jobs keep their operator state inside the per-job
[`ContinuousWindowExecutor`] — snapshotting the executor-wide generic
backend for them would persist vacuous state (the window operators never
write to it).  This enum makes the selection explicit and typed instead of
hiding it behind a partially implemented `StateBackend` adapter.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Backend)

### Backend([Arc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/sync/struct.Arc.html)<[Mutex](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/sync/poison/mutex/struct.Mutex.html)<[Box](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/boxed/struct.Box.html)<dyn [StateBackend](https://docs.rs/krishiv-state/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/krishiv_state/backend/trait.StateBackend.html)>>>)

Generic keyed state backend shared by non-window stateful tasks.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ContinuousWindow)

### ContinuousWindow([Arc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/sync/struct.Arc.html)<[Mutex](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/sync/poison/mutex/struct.Mutex.html)<[ContinuousWindowExecutor](https://docs.rs/krishiv-dataflow/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/krishiv_dataflow/continuous/struct.ContinuousWindowExecutor.html)>>)

Stateful continuous window executor owned by a `stream:loop:` job.

```
pub enum ExecutorTaskOutputKind {
    Sql,
    ConnectorPipeline,
    Cancelled,
    ShuffleWrite,
    StreamingWindow,
    IvmStep,
}
```
## Expand description

Local executor output kind.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Sql)

### Sql

Real SQL fragment executed through the Krishiv SQL/DataFusion seam.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ConnectorPipeline)

### ConnectorPipeline

Connector-to-connector pipeline executed by the task runner.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Cancelled)

### Cancelled

Task was cancelled before execution started.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ShuffleWrite)

### ShuffleWrite

Shuffle write: hash-partitioned batches written to the local shuffle store.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.StreamingWindow)

### StreamingWindow

Streaming window aggregation output (tumbling, sliding, or session).

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.IvmStep)

### IvmStep

One bounded IVM tick completed (DeltaBatch model).
